hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on the posted salary range as the ceiling for negotiation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Employers sometimes post ranges lower than their true budget; the posted range is a floor, not a ceiling — negotiating above it is possible with market data justification
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates in BC and Ontario who assume the posted range represents the maximum offer

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a Level I or Level II wage level on an H-1B filing
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Under the wage-weighted lottery effective February 27, 2026, Level I filings receive only 1 lottery entry vs. 4 entries for Level IV — substantially lower selection probability without any change in eligibility requirements
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: H-1B cap-subject candidates whose employers file at low wage levels, particularly entry-level candidates who may qualify for Level III or IV based on actual duties

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using BC-specific salary history deflection scripts when interviewing for an Ontario role
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Ontario does not have a salary history ban; an employer asking about prior pay in Ontario is acting legally, and framing your refusal as a legal right would be inaccurate
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who move between provinces or receive advice calibrated to BC law and apply it uniformly across Canada

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Filing a PERM application for Indian nationals in EB-2 category
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The employer must ensure the offered wage meets the prevailing wage at the time the worker actually receives the visa — for Indian EB-2 nationals, current estimates place the visa wait at 134+ years, making wage compliance at time of visa receipt practically unachievable
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Indian nationals in EB-2 PERM pipeline; employers sponsoring Indian nationals for EB-2 green cards

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Assuming pay transparency rules apply to all Canadian employers
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Alberta and Quebec have not enacted job posting salary range disclosure requirements as of mid-2026; candidates in those provinces cannot rely on posted ranges as a negotiation anchor because the employer has no obligation to post them
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates applying to roles in Alberta or Quebec who expect the same transparency protections as BC or Ontario

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating salary to Level IV threshold for H-1B filing
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The salary increase of approximately $30,000 (e.g., $181,210 to $211,100 for SF Software Developer) also changes the lottery entry count from 3 to 4 — meaning the negotiation outcome affects not just compensation but also the probability of H-1B selection
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: H-1B candidates whose employers would otherwise file at Level III; applies only to H-1B visa holders, not US citizens or permanent residents

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using Government of Canada Job Bank wage data as a proxy for total compensation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Job Bank Canada captures base salary using Statistics Canada Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours data and may undercount total compensation including bonuses and equity
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates in tech or professional roles where total compensation (equity, bonuses) significantly exceeds base salary

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on OEWS-derived prevailing wage without checking employer's actual LCA history
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The OFLC performance data reveals what the employer has actually paid for comparable roles in prior filings — this may be substantially higher than the OEWS minimum floor, and the candidate negotiating only to the floor leaves verifiable employer-specific data unused
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: H-1B candidates who benchmark only against DOL minimums rather than employer-disclosed actual wages

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Assuming Ontario's pay transparency law covers all Ontario employers from January 1, 2026
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Ontario's Working for Workers Four Act, 2024 applies only to employers with 25 or more employees; employers below that threshold are not required to post salary ranges
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates applying to small Ontario employers or startups with fewer than 25 employees

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an offer at Wage Level I or II without negotiating up to the next threshold
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Under the new system, a Level I candidate has approximately half the lottery odds of a Level IV candidate — accepting a lower wage level is not just a compensation concession, it is a probabilistic concession on immigration outcome
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Entry-level H-1B candidates who are unaware of the wage-weighted system and negotiate only on compensation grounds without considering lottery probability

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Disclosing your current salary when asked — even when legal — to appear cooperative or avoid awkwardness
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The number becomes a hard anchor that bounds the offer regardless of the role's actual budget; even a generous employer will rarely offer far above a disclosed current salary
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Underpaid candidates, career changers moving to higher-paying industries, and anyone whose current comp is below market rate for the new role

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a Canadian tech role over a US FAANG offer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: At senior levels, the total compensation gap is severe — a senior SWE earns $150K–$220K CAD ($110K–$161K USD) in Canada vs. $250K–$400K USD at US FAANG. Over a 5-year career the gap can exceed $500K–$1M USD in forgone earnings.
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High-performing senior engineers who qualify for US FAANG roles but choose Canada for immigration stability or lifestyle reasons

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Framing a salary negotiation purely around market data rather than wage level thresholds
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You may successfully negotiate a $5,000–$10,000 increase that stays within the same wage level, gaining purchasing power but zero improvement in lottery selection probability
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: H-1B candidates who do not research DOL prevailing wage thresholds before negotiating and therefore leave the most asymmetric value on the table

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Not knowing your state's salary history ban status before interviewing
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You may comply with an illegal question, forfeit your legal protections through voluntary disclosure, and lose negotiating leverage that the law was explicitly designed to give you
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time job seekers and anyone relocating to a new state who hasn't updated their knowledge of local employment law

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating with US salary data in a Canadian interview process
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You appear out of touch with Canadian market norms, which signals poor market research to the recruiter and can damage your candidacy even if your target number is individually reasonable
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students or recent US-based candidates who apply to Canadian roles without recalibrating their salary expectations to the Canadian market

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating a higher salary without confirming the job duties will support the higher wage level classification
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The employer's attorney may file the LCA at a lower wage level regardless of salary, meaning the candidate receives more pay but no additional lottery entries — and may face LCA compliance issues
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who assume salary and wage level are directly correlated and do not verify the duties-based classification with immigration counsel

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Escalating a salary history ban violation to the state labor department or pursuing legal action
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: While legally valid, it almost certainly ends your candidacy with that employer and may create reputational risk in tight-knit industries or geographies
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are actively job searching in a narrow industry where the employer has significant market presence

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Focusing negotiation only on base salary in Canada
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The most movable component (signing bonus) goes unasked, and the highest-value component at FAANG Canada (RSU grants) goes unoptimized — both represent more negotiable upside than base
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Junior and mid-level candidates negotiating their first Canadian tech offer, who default to base salary as the only lever

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on the wage-weighted lottery rule as settled law for long-term career planning
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The rule faces potential legal challenges that could result in injunctions before the FY2027 lottery, leaving candidates who negotiated specifically around wage levels without the expected immigration benefit
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who have structured their entire compensation negotiation strategy around the wage-level lottery differential before the rule survives legal challenge

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on a ban-state employer voluntarily following the law without knowing your rights
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Violations are common; without knowing what's prohibited, you cannot recognize when a violation occurs, let alone document or respond to it
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who assume legal compliance without verification, particularly those earlier in their careers who treat recruiter questions as standard procedure

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking a Montreal role because the salary looks close to Toronto after reading the job posting
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Montreal salaries are structurally 15–25% below Toronto; bilingual requirements can also constrain future mobility within the Montreal market for non-French speakers
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates relocating to Montreal from other provinces or countries who don't adjust for the structural salary discount

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Reframing a voluntarily disclosed low salary upward mid-process
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: While strategically sound, it can create friction with the recruiter and signal inconsistency — the reframe must be tied to new information (role scope, market data) to land credibly
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who disclosed early without leverage or context and are now trying to recover lost ground

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting the first offer at a Canadian established company after being told 'the band is set'
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The signing bonus — which is expected to be asked for at Canadian tech companies — is left entirely on the table, representing $5K–$20K+ in immediately accessible compensation
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time negotiators who take 'the band is set' as a signal that all negotiation is closed

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Comparing a Calgary gross salary offer directly to a Toronto gross salary offer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Alberta's absence of provincial income tax means the Calgary offer is worth 8–12% more in take-home than the identical gross in Toronto — ignoring this makes Calgary look worse than it is
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates choosing between Alberta and Ontario/BC roles who evaluate offers by gross salary alone

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying with LMIA-sponsoring employer past PGWP expiry without achieving PR
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You become employer-tied at the exact moment your career leverage should be increasing; your job market effectively shrinks to only LMIA-capable employers, and your ability to walk away from a bad compensation situation disappears
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PGWP holders who delay CEC Express Entry applications or who fail to accumulate NOC TEER 0/1 experience quickly enough

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a retention counter-offer from your current employer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: 80% of people who accept counter-offers leave within 12 months anyway — the underlying reasons for considering leaving typically remain unresolved
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Anyone who is leaving for non-compensation reasons (growth ceiling, culture, management) but gets matched on salary

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a retention counter-offer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The company now knows you're a flight risk and may deprioritize you for promotions, key projects, or new responsibilities while quietly searching for your replacement
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People who accepted for comp reasons while the root cause was scope, manager fit, or career ceiling — they stay but the dynamic is permanently altered

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Pushing to a fourth or fifth negotiation round
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You enter day one with the perception of being a difficult or extractive employee, which can subtly affect your manager's advocacy for you in future reviews
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who optimize for maximum extraction without understanding the relationship cost

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating over email instead of requesting a phone call
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Recruiter can respond with a templated 'no' in seconds with no social friction — the path of least resistance is always to decline in writing
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People who are conflict-averse and prefer written communication, believing it is more comfortable or professional

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an inflated title at a startup
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Future large-company employers will benchmark you against that inflated title level and find you don't meet the scope expectations, potentially downleveling you and suppressing comp
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early-career professionals who use startup title inflation as a stepping stone to large tech companies

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a signing bonus with a cliff clawback and spending it
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You create a financial liability that persists for the entire clawback period. If laid off before the cliff, you owe the gross amount — which may exceed what you actually have available to repay
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early-career employees who receive large signing bonuses relative to their savings, and employees at companies with high layoff risk

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting the first offer to avoid friction and preserve the sponsorship relationship
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Systematically under-negotiating by 10–30% relative to domestic peers, which compounds over a career to hundreds of thousands of dollars in lost compensation
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students on OPT and early H-1B holders who conflate sponsorship preservation with salary acceptance

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Revealing your current salary when asked
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The company can now anchor your offer to your past underpayment rather than your market value; you've effectively justified a below-market offer by providing evidence that you've accepted below-market pay before
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are currently underpaid relative to market, early-career professionals, and those switching from lower-paying industries or geographies

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a high signing bonus as part of the offer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The signing bonus inflates the perceived total comp, masking a below-market annual salary; once you model year 2 comp without it, the offer may be substantially weaker than alternatives
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early-career candidates who are cash-constrained and anchor emotionally on the large one-time number

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Disclosing LMIA need early in the application process to startups
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Screening occurs before you can demonstrate value; you lose the chance to convert genuine interest into an offer that creates negotiation context
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who need LMIA and are applying to early-stage or growth-stage companies without established immigration infrastructure

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Countering with a signing bonus instead of base when base is locked
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Signing bonus is immediate cash but does not compound — it does not raise the baseline for future raises, bonuses, or equity refreshes, which are all anchored to base salary
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates planning to stay long-term at a company where annual raises and refresh grants are base-dependent

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking an internal transfer at the same level mid-promo-cycle
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Your promotion eligibility clock resets, potentially pushing your next promotion 2+ years out even though you accepted what looked like a lateral move
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High performers who are 6–12 months into a promo cycle and don't calculate the full timeline cost before accepting

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Manufacturing a fake competing offer to gain leverage
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Recruiters verify offers and if caught, the offer is typically rescinded and your professional reputation in that company's network is damaged
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates without real competing offers who feel pressured to fabricate one

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Giving a salary range instead of a single number when counter-offering
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The company anchors to the bottom of your range and treats it as your actual ask, not a midpoint
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who believe showing flexibility signals reasonableness — it actually signals willingness to accept the lower number

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating all levers simultaneously
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Signals extraction-maximizing behavior to the recruiter and hiring manager, which can sour goodwill and make them less likely to advocate for you internally
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are negotiating their first offer and conflate thoroughness with effectiveness

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Signing a clawback clause without reading the termination trigger language
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A clause with 'for any reason or no reason' language means a layoff — an event entirely outside your control — triggers full repayment. You can be both unemployed and indebted simultaneously.
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Anyone joining a company in a volatile industry, recently-funded startup, or large tech company with a history of reductions in force

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Disclosing visa status early in the application process to be transparent
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Sponsorship cost becomes a filter that eliminates you before your qualifications are assessed — you lose the evaluation before the competition begins
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who interpret transparency as an early-stage obligation rather than a strategic timing decision

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting the first offer immediately without countering
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You signal that you either didn't know negotiation was possible or didn't believe you had standing to negotiate — which experienced hiring managers interpret as a competence signal about your professional self-awareness
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time job seekers and engineers who have internalized the cultural norm that discussing compensation is unseemly

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking a startup offer with significant equity upside
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Options with a 90-day exercise window create a golden handcuff: leaving the company means either paying out-of-pocket to exercise vested options (often tens of thousands of dollars) or forfeiting them entirely
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates with limited liquid savings who cannot afford to exercise options when leaving, effectively trapping them regardless of job satisfaction

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating weakly on first Canadian job offer as PGWP holder due to assumed future LMIA dependency
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If you execute the clean PGWP → CEC → PR timeline, you had full mobility the entire time and left money on the table unnecessarily; the assumed leverage the employer had was never real
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who understand immigration at a surface level but don't map their specific timeline against PR eligibility thresholds

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating equity and base simultaneously in the first exchange
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Muddying the negotiation with total comp math reduces clarity and gives the recruiter room to trade off components against each other unfavorably
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are less experienced at negotiation and do not realize that sequential negotiation of components preserves more leverage

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating for internal promotion without an external offer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Manager can delay with vague promises ('we'll make it right at your next review') with no accountability, and you're locked in mid-cycle unable to credibly threaten to leave
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Loyal employees who prefer stability and haven't maintained external market optionality

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an offer without knowing your BATNA
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You lose the ability to walk away when you should, meaning you may accept a package below your actual floor because you have no pre-committed reference point
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time negotiators and people who are emotionally attached to a specific offer or company

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Expressing full enthusiasm for a promotion before discussing compensation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You implicitly signal acceptance of the role under any terms, eliminating your negotiating leverage before comp is even discussed
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High performers who are excited and grateful for recognition and lead with emotion before thinking strategically

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a signing bonus without reading the clawback provision
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If you leave within 12–24 months for any reason — including being laid off or hating the role — you may owe back the full amount, creating a financial trap that delays exit
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates at companies with high attrition or instability, and those who may be evaluating the role as a short-term stepping stone

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Not negotiating gross vs. net repayment terms
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If you trigger the clawback, you repay more than you ever received. On a $30K bonus, you net $20K but owe $30K — creating a $10K deficit from a bonus you no longer have.
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Any employee who triggers a clawback, but hits hardest on those in high tax brackets or with large bonuses

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Treating H-1B dependency as a permanent lock-in that prevents job switching
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Employers who understand that you believe you cannot leave will price your comp accordingly — the psychological trap becomes a real financial one even if the legal constraint is softer than believed
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: H-1B holders who don't know about the 60-day portability rule and therefore cannot credibly imply alternatives

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating only on base salary
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You leave significant value on the table in dimensions where companies have far more flexibility — signing bonuses, equity, vacation, professional development, remote work — while fighting hardest on the dimension most constrained by HR pay bands
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Anyone whose salary ask hits a hard company ceiling but who doesn't know to redirect to other levers

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating via email instead of phone to feel less confrontational
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The recruiter cannot advocate internally on your behalf in real time; email reduces them to a passive relay and removes the social dynamic that makes recruiters want to 'fight for you'
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Introverted or conflict-averse candidates who default to written communication as a comfort mechanism

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using employer LMIA investment argument in a new job negotiation (rather than a retention context)
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The argument lacks credibility because the new employer has no sunk cost — it can come across as trying to import a relationship asset that doesn't exist yet, weakening rather than strengthening the ask
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who successfully used the LMIA investment argument internally and attempt to replicate it in external offer negotiations

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Continuing to push after a company says 'this is our final offer' without new leverage
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Risks damaging the relationship with the hiring team even if the offer is not withdrawn
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who have already met 90%+ of their target but push for marginal gains beyond the final offer threshold

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Revealing an external offer to your current employer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Even if you stay via counter-offer, you've permanently signaled disloyalty — future career advancement may be quietly impeded
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People who use the external offer as a negotiation tactic but genuinely intend to stay long-term

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Backing out of an accepted offer after receiving a competing offer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: While there is no legal liability before a start date, there is a real reputational cost that can follow you, especially in tight-knit industries or if the recruiter moves to another company
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates in small industries or who may encounter the same recruiters again

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a verbal commitment on signing bonus or remote work without written confirmation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The commitment has no legal enforceability and the specific person who made it may not be around when you join
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who build trust-based relationships with recruiters and assume goodwill will carry through to onboarding

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on a verbal remote work agreement instead of written confirmation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Hiring manager or team changes post-joining mean the agreement has no enforcement mechanism; you may be called back to office with no recourse
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Anyone who chose the role primarily because of remote flexibility and whose next-best alternative was a fully remote position

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a 24-month clawback period without negotiating down
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Your career mobility is suppressed for two years. Leaving for a better opportunity within 24 months — a normal career move — carries full or partial financial penalty.
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High performers who may receive outside offers, and employees whose role changes significantly (restructuring, manager changes) but who want to leave before 24 months

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a sponsorship commitment without verifying execution infrastructure
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You may sign and onboard only to discover the company has no immigration counsel, has never completed an H-1B, and cannot actually deliver the sponsorship — leaving you in status limbo
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who distinguish sponsorship willingness from execution capacity too late — after accepting the offer

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Letting an exploding offer deadline pass without explicitly challenging it
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The offer lapses; the assumption that 'they'll still want me' is almost always wrong because the company interprets silence as disinterest or indecisiveness, not as a negotiating move
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are conflict-averse and assume the company will proactively extend without being asked

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Reneging on an accepted offer after signing
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: While legal consequences are minimal, reputation damage within the industry is real and persistent, particularly in small or tight-knit sectors where recruiters and hiring managers move between companies
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates in niche technical domains or geographic markets where professional networks are dense and interconnected

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a bridging open work permit without verifying whether it remains tied to original employer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A bridging open work permit tied to the original employer provides the appearance of mobility without the reality; leaving the employer may void work authorization even though the permit says 'open'
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates in late-stage PR application processes who believe they have full mobility because their permit says 'open'

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Disclosing the competing company name when using a competing offer as leverage
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Not required and potentially harmful — you have leverage from the number alone; disclosing the company name adds no benefit and may create complications
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates negotiating between companies in the same industry or network where relationships between hiring teams exist

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Waiting for the annual review cycle to address a significant comp gap
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Comp gaps compound over time — a 20% underpayment left unaddressed for 2–3 years becomes structural underpayment that's harder to correct in a single cycle
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High performers at companies with modest annual raise percentages who don't proactively request off-cycle market corrections

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using speed creation ('I'll sign today if you hit X') as a closing tactic
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If the company calls your bluff and doesn't move, you've either signed at a number you settled for or you must back down, weakening your credibility in the negotiation
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who use urgency tactics without being genuinely prepared to follow through

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Countering on multiple items simultaneously
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: It signals that no single concession will close the deal, which reduces recruiter motivation to push internally for any of them
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Analytically-minded candidates who want to optimize everything at once and believe comprehensive asks are efficient

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating a delayed start date to capture unvested equity
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Your review cycle at the new company starts later, potentially pushing your first performance review and raise eligibility out by months
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates joining companies with strict annual review cycles where start month determines review eligibility

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Treating the signing bonus as equivalent to salary when comparing offers
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The signing bonus carries clawback risk that salary does not. Comparing a $20K salary increase to a $20K signing bonus ignores that the bonus is contingent and reversible.
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates evaluating competing offers where one uses a large signing bonus to close a compensation gap

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Framing long-term visa commitment as a weakness during negotiation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You surrender a genuine retention differentiator — the fact that you are likely to stay 2–3 years longer than domestic peers — and allow the employer to use it as leverage instead of you using it as value
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who have internalized the visa constraint as purely negative and haven't been exposed to the reframe

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Making a specific salary counter-request early in negotiation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You reveal your floor — the company now knows the minimum you'll accept and can offer just above it rather than their true ceiling
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who mistake specificity for confidence; particularly harms those who would have received higher offers if they had maintained information asymmetry

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using levels.fyi data without specifying level in the negotiation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Being vague about comp targets while citing market data allows the recruiter to assume a lower level benchmark; specificity about level is required for the data to support your ask
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who research market rates but fail to confirm which level their offer corresponds to

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a promotion verbally without written criteria or comp terms
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The promotion can be delayed, rescoped, or undercompensated with no recourse — verbal promises have no enforceability when managers change or budgets shift
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Employees who trust manager relationships and don't formalize agreements in writing

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Framing post-acceptance negotiation as a comp ask without performance data
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: It signals to your manager that you were strategically underbidding at hire, which can erode trust even if the ask is granted
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: New employees who attempt post-acceptance negotiation too early or without clear delivery evidence

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Not asking for an extension on an exploding offer deadline
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You make a consequential financial decision without adequate market comparison data, and implicitly accept terms that may have been improvable with one more competing offer
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who fear appearing difficult or non-committal, especially those who are relieved to have any offer

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking unlimited PTO instead of negotiating a guaranteed PTO floor
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Unlimited PTO policies often result in employees taking less vacation than those with defined allocations due to social pressure and ambiguity about norms
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates coming from cultures or roles where rest and personal time are already underprotected

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Running a single-company job search to preserve OPT time
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You eliminate competing offer leverage entirely, capping your negotiating ceiling at whatever the single company is willing to offer without external market pressure
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: OPT students who are risk-averse about timeline and underestimate the financial return of a multi-process search

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Treating negotiation as a one-shot transaction focused only on the current offer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You optimize for the immediate package while ignoring that the number sets your raise baseline and your next employer's anchor; short-term framing systematically undervalues the compounding effect of early-career negotiations
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early-career professionals who are focused on getting the offer rather than optimizing lifetime earnings

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Prioritizing base salary in negotiation when base is capped
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Spending political capital pushing against a fixed base leaves signing bonus and equity refresh untouched; these alternative levers are often approvable without escalation but are never offered proactively
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time negotiators who treat base salary as the only meaningful dimension of compensation

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using personal financial need as the primary justification for a higher salary
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The employer is not buying your expenses — they are buying your labor; need-based justifications are weak because they don't connect to your value, and they can create perception of financial desperation that weakens your leverage
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates with genuine financial pressure (student loans, relocation costs, family obligations) who frame it as their primary argument rather than as a supporting detail alongside market data

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Fabricating or exaggerating a competing offer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Recruiters have access to detailed compensation benchmarks and professional networks; they can often detect implausible offers, and being caught in dishonesty permanently damages the relationship and can rescind the real offer
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates with no real competing offers who feel pressure to manufacture leverage

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Applying to remote-only roles to maximize job options
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Many remote roles on Canadian job boards are US-remote only or exclude PGWP holders due to employer uncertainty about cross-border compliance; response rates drop significantly vs. roles tied to a Canadian office
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Internationally-educated PGWP holders who assume 'remote' is the same across all Canadian job postings

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a role without verifying its NOC TEER classification
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The work experience may not qualify for Canadian Experience Class, delaying CEC eligibility and the entire PR timeline
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International graduates on PGWP who are counting on CEC as their primary PR pathway and have limited time on their permit

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Being transparent about future H-1B need during early rounds
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Companies that wouldn't sponsor may screen you out before evaluating your skills, even though you are fully authorized to work for 1-3 years on OPT/STEM OPT
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students early in job search who disclose too early out of anxiety or perceived obligation

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Applying exclusively through job board portals as an international student
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Job portals route resumes through ATS and HR screens that filter on visa sponsorship before a human sees the application; OP reported approximately 1% callback rate via this channel
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students on OPT or PGWP who lack referrals and are competing against domestic candidates at the screening stage

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a highly-cited advisor at a top-ranked program without checking their industry connections
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Students may complete a strong academic PhD but find themselves in postdoc limbo rather than industry research roles, because the advisor had no industry collaborations or internship pipeline to leverage
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students at top-5 programs who assumed program prestige alone would open industry research doors

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using F-1 re-enrollment as a bridge to extend stay and reset OPT eligibility
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You must genuinely pursue the degree (not just enroll), you lose career momentum and seniority, and the timeline to regain work authorization through a new OPT application adds further delay
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career professionals on STEM OPT who have been in industry 1–3 years and would face significant opportunity cost from returning to school

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a large RSU grant from a pre-IPO startup
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: At IPO, the entire accumulated unvested RSU value is taxed as ordinary income in a single year, potentially pushing the employee into the highest tax bracket — effectively losing ~50% of the grant value to taxes
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Employees who joined a startup years before IPO and have accumulated a large RSU balance

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Underquoting your salary expectation to seem more hireable
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You anchor all future raises, bonuses, and pension contributions to a lower base — the cumulative loss over time far exceeds the short-term hiring advantage
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career professionals (2–5 years experience) who are optimizing for getting the offer rather than long-term earnings

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing the higher-salary offer without considering role type
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A higher-paying QA/testing role locks you into a lower-value job category, making future salary jumps harder even if current pay is better than an algorithm or data engineering role
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early-career candidates who optimize for immediate income over role-based career capital
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_接到了不同的_OFFER_应该怎么比较.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a low base salary with the expectation of catching up through performance raises
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Salary increases at most companies are percentage-based, so a lower base permanently compounds into lower absolute pay even with identical performance ratings — the gap never closes organically
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: New hires who negotiated poorly at offer stage and are counting on internal raises to correct the gap

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an unsatisfactory offer without negotiating, planning to 'prove yourself' and ask for more after joining
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Salary adjustments in large companies are tied to fixed review windows; you cannot negotiate outside those windows, and by the time the window opens you are already bound by the contract you signed
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: New hires at large tech companies or corporations with formal HR cycles (most US and Canadian big tech)
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_收到offer了还能不能再谈薪资.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting RSUs at a startup that then goes bankrupt
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Because RSU income is taxed as ordinary income at vest time, employees who vest RSUs at a company that subsequently fails have already paid income tax on shares that are now worthless — a permanent loss with no tax recovery equivalent to the option holder's ability to simply not exercise
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Employees at pre-IPO companies that grant RSUs rather than options, particularly those who vest shortly before a company downturn
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_求问美国it公司的rsu和bonus是怎么回事.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving compensation details vague during early recruiter calls to avoid 'anchoring low'
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: After the offer is issued, trying to add overlooked components (13th month, meal stipend, housing benefit) feels like bad faith to the recruiter and can collapse the deal entirely
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are disorganized about their own compensation or who assume the recruiter will figure it out
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_面试时谈薪的技巧有些什么啊.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using LinkedIn Easy Apply for high-volume roles at large companies
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Applications enter an ATS queue competing with 500+ other applicants, effectively making the application invisible without a referral or direct recruiter contact; effort spent here has near-zero return
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: New PGWP job seekers who optimize for application volume over application quality and network leverage

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Skipping French language preparation because English is already strong
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Leaving 25–50+ CRS points on the table, which can mean the difference between receiving an ITA in competitive draws versus waiting years or never receiving one
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Express Entry candidates with moderate CRS scores who are sitting just below the typical cutoff for their category

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a company's 'no sponsorship' statement at face value
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You may disqualify yourself from roles where STEM OPT extension would have been acceptable — the company's policy only excludes H-1B, not OPT paperwork
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: STEM OPT-eligible candidates with 1-3 years of additional authorization who prematurely self-filter

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Emailing HR directly for cold outreach
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: HR filters on sponsorship requirements as part of their screening function, often resulting in no response even for strong candidates; the rejection happens before skills are ever evaluated
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who assume HR is the correct first point of contact for job inquiries

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Pursuing a funded PhD intending to become a software engineer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The PhD credential provides minimal salary or role premium for SWE positions, while costing 4-5 years of compounding earnings, promotions, and industry experience that peers who entered directly have accumulated
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: CS students who pursue a PhD as a prestige signal or default path without a specific research or faculty career goal

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a job offer with only a verbal promise of H-1B sponsorship
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Company policy can change at any time after hire, leaving you with no legal recourse and a compressed timeline to find a new sponsor — the original poster discovered this 18 months into the role
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Any international worker on OPT at any stage, but especially those who trusted employer reputation over explicit contractual language

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Early exercising ISO options at a startup
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If the company's stock later drops (as in the 2000 dot-com crash), the employee still owes AMT (Alternative Minimum Tax) calculated on the paper gain at exercise time, even though the stock is now worthless — leading to tax bills exceeding the actual value of shares held
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Employees at high-growth startups who early-exercise ISO options anticipating IPO gains
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_受限股票单位_RSU_与股票期权_Stock_Option_的区别有哪些.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Declining to disclose your expected salary and asking HR to name a number first
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: HR cannot quote a final number before knowing your expectations — so this tactic forces HR to either stall the process or make an uninformed internal recommendation, reducing the chance of a good outcome for you
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who have read negotiation advice telling them 'never show your cards first' and apply it rigidly
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_应聘时何时适合谈薪资.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a prestigious large company for the brand value
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Some large companies have very low internal mobility — employees sit at the same level for 3-4 years with minimal raises, negating the brand benefit and losing years of compounding salary growth
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career professionals who assume prestige always translates to growth
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_接到了不同的_OFFER_应该怎么比较.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining at a salary you are unhappy with and trying to leave shortly after
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Short tenure is interpreted as either performance failure or poor decision-making by future employers; you also bear switching costs — relocation, gap in bonus/vesting, re-onboarding time
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who rationalized the low offer as temporary and did not negotiate at the offer stage
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_收到offer了还能不能再谈薪资.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying at a company until the full 4-year RSU cliff without negotiating equity refresh
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: At the 2-year mark, the employee's forward-looking compensation drops sharply (from e.g., 125K/year to 100K/year projected), making them financially vulnerable to being poached — but many employees don't realize this until they do the math themselves
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-level employees who accepted strong initial RSU packages but never asked about or received equity refresh grants
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_求问美国it公司的rsu和bonus是怎么回事.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a salary figure that seems like a 20–30% raise over monthly base
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The raise disappears or reverses when the new company pays 12 months vs. 13, has lower bonus averages, lower social insurance contributions, or removes non-monetary benefits like subsidized housing or meal cards
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who compare only headline monthly base figures without converting to total annual compensation
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_面试时谈薪的技巧有些什么啊.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Treating the Canadian job search identically to the US international student job search (emphasizing visa status upfront)
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Unnecessarily flagging yourself as a potential sponsorship burden when PGWP requires zero employer action, reducing callback rates
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International graduates who studied in both countries or followed US-centric advice from peers or online communities

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Waiting until after offer acceptance to raise sponsorship
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If the company cannot sponsor, you must reject an offer you've already negotiated, burning goodwill and potentially foreclosing future opportunities at that company
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who avoid the conversation out of fear and delay until it becomes costly

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Disclosing visa/OPT status upfront in a cold email
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The recipient processes the sponsorship requirement as a cost and risk before they have any reason to value the candidate; the email is closed before skills are read
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who believe transparency about constraints builds trust early in outreach

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving a startup before options vest
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Standard 90-day exercise window after departure forces an immediate cash decision: pay the full strike price plus anticipated tax, or forfeit all vested options
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Employees at startups with standard short exercise windows, especially those who have vested options with significant spread but limited personal liquidity
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_受限股票单位_RSU_与股票期权_Stock_Option_的区别有哪些.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a platform/brand name company at a salary discount
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You lose the income immediately, and the 'prestige value' only materializes if future employers actually value that brand — which is not guaranteed in all industries
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early-to-mid career professionals who prioritize resume signaling over current compensation
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_应聘时何时适合谈薪资.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an offer with attractive unvested equity or promised future raises
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: These are non-guaranteed and should not be counted as real compensation; people who factor them in overestimate their actual total comp and make suboptimal comparisons
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Anyone comparing offers that differ significantly in equity or raise promises
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_接到了不同的_OFFER_应该怎么比较.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Not negotiating because you 'don't want to cause trouble' for the hiring manager
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You absorb all the cost of the manager's internal process, while the manager and company retain the full benefit of your labor at below-market rate
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Risk-averse candidates, international students, and fresh graduates who fear rejection
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_收到offer了还能不能再谈薪资.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving a company with vested ISO options without planning the exercise
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The 90-day post-termination exercise window requires immediate cash outlay of potentially $10K–$100K+ to exercise vested options, with AMT tax exposure on top. Many employees forfeit valuable vested options simply because they lack the liquidity
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early employees at fast-growing private companies who have accumulated significant vested options but limited liquid savings
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_求问美国it公司的rsu和bonus是怎么回事.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating purely on base salary while ignoring bonus structure
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: At companies where bonus is a large share of total comp, winning a higher base but accepting a lower expected bonus can result in lower total comp than an alternative offer with lower base but reliable bonus
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates at companies or levels where bonus is material (finance, tech, senior roles)
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_面试时谈薪的技巧有些什么啊.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Prioritizing base salary over equity when evaluating offers
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: In Silicon Valley/Bay Area tech, the compounding upside of equity — especially at pre-IPO companies — can dwarf total base salary over a multi-year period; optimizing for base salary alone can mean leaving very large sums on the table
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: New graduates and international candidates who focus on the certainty of base pay and discount equity as speculative
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_受限股票单位_RSU_与股票期权_Stock_Option_的区别有哪些.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving a job in Q4 to start a new one before annual bonus payout
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You forfeit that year's annual bonus — which can represent 1–3 months of additional income — for no gain
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Anyone considering a job change in October–December who has not accounted for bonus timing
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_应聘时何时适合谈薪资.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Ignoring commute time to capture a higher salary
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: 2-3 hour daily commutes produce compounding fatigue and life-quality loss that no salary premium fully compensates for; the psychological toll accumulates invisibly
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People who rationally weigh salary but underweight daily time costs
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_接到了不同的_OFFER_应该怎么比较.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Exercising ISOs and holding shares to qualify for long-term capital gains treatment
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Holding exercised ISO shares triggers AMT (Alternative Minimum Tax) liability in the exercise year, even though no cash has been received — creating a tax bill without liquidity to pay it
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High-earning employees at well-valued private companies who exercise large ISO blocks hoping to convert to long-term capital gains
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_求问美国it公司的rsu和bonus是怎么回事.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Verbally accepting or strongly signaling acceptance before clarifying all terms
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Once the recruiter believes the deal is done, they lose motivation to re-open any aspect of it; asking to adjust afterward is perceived as reneging and damages the relationship
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are conflict-averse and signal agreement prematurely to avoid tension
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_面试时谈薪的技巧有些什么啊.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Prioritizing a well-aligned team culture over immediate compensation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The benefit is invisible when things are good but becomes the dominant factor when things go wrong — the 'spiritual damage cost' (精神损失费) of a misaligned team is systematically underestimated at decision time
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who treat culture as a soft/optional factor in an otherwise transactional comparison
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_接到了不同的_OFFER_应该怎么比较.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a role based on nominal RSU grant value stated in the offer letter
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The number of shares is not fixed at offer time — it is determined on the first day of employment based on the stock price that day. If the stock price rises between offer acceptance and start date, the employee receives fewer shares than mentally modeled
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time offer recipients at public tech companies who do not understand that dollar value is fixed but share count floats
hidden_tradeoffs._source: zhihu_求问美国it公司的rsu和bonus是怎么回事.txt

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on verbal promises about future salary increases or performance bonuses as part of the total package
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Verbal commitments are unenforceable; the source explicitly flags that year-end bonuses paid in June of the following year, discretionary raises, and unwritten equity grants may never materialize
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time job changers or anyone joining a company without verifying what is written into the contract
