failure_patterns.pattern: BC employer asks about applicant's pay history during the hiring process
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18 explicitly prohibits asking about pay history at any point in the hiring process and prohibits using pay history to set starting wages
failure_patterns.consequence: Director of Employment Standards can investigate complaints; employer can face orders to pay compensation to the affected applicant
warning_signs: Recruiter or hiring manager asks 'What are you currently making?' during a BC hiring process
Employer references prior salary to justify a lower initial offer in BC

failure_patterns.pattern: Employer pays below the prevailing wage for the certified SOC code, wage level, and MSA
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: INA Section 212(n) and 20 CFR Part 655 require the employer to pay at least the prevailing wage as a condition of the H-1B; underpayment violates the Labor Condition Agreement (LCA)
failure_patterns.consequence: LCA violation; potential debarment of employer from future H-1B filings; back wage liability to the worker
warning_signs: Employer offers compensation below the published FLC Data Center threshold for the applicable SOC, MSA, and level
Employer uses a lower wage level classification than the job duties would support to reduce minimum wage obligation

failure_patterns.pattern: BC employer retaliates against an employee for discussing their pay with coworkers
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18 explicitly prohibits retaliation against employees who discuss their pay with coworkers
failure_patterns.consequence: Director of Employment Standards can investigate; employer can face enforcement action and orders to pay compensation
warning_signs: Disciplinary action taken against an employee shortly after they discussed salary with a colleague
Policy prohibiting employees from discussing compensation with peers

failure_patterns.pattern: Wage level assigned does not match actual job duties
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: DOL defines wage levels by job complexity and supervision criteria; misclassifying a complex independent role as Level I to reduce wage obligation constitutes an LCA misrepresentation
failure_patterns.consequence: LCA violation; DOL audit liability; potential H-1B denial or revocation
warning_signs: Employer assigns Level I to a role requiring independent judgment and complex decision-making
Job description on LCA does not match actual duties performed by the worker

failure_patterns.pattern: Ontario employer with 25+ employees fails to include compensation range in job postings on or after January 1, 2026
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Working for Workers Four Act, 2024, S.O. 2024, c. 15, Schedule 2 requires compensation range disclosure for all Ontario postings (public and internal) for covered employers
failure_patterns.consequence: Employment Standards Officer can issue compliance orders and penalties
warning_signs: Ontario job posting by a 25+ employee employer dated after January 1, 2026 that omits salary information
Internal job posting visible to employees that lacks compensation range after the effective date

failure_patterns.pattern: Using outdated prevailing wage data from a prior year when filing LCA
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: BLS updates OEWS data annually; the FLC Data Center reflects the current year's thresholds; prior-year values may be below the currently applicable prevailing wage
failure_patterns.consequence: LCA filed with an insufficient wage commitment; potential wage violation if the worker is paid below the current prevailing wage
warning_signs: Wage figures used in LCA match prior-year FLC Data Center values rather than the current year
Employer relies on internally cached wage tables rather than verifying at flcdatacenter.com

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating salary as if you are a US citizen — optimizing only for total comp without accounting for wage level thresholds
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Most salary negotiation advice is written for US citizens or permanent residents; H-1B candidates apply the same frameworks without adjusting for the asymmetric value of crossing a wage level boundary
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidate may secure a modest raise but remain at Wage Level II, missing a 50% increase in lottery selection probability for the difference of $15,000–$30,000 in salary
warning_signs: Candidate references only market data (Levels, Glassdoor, competing offers) without mentioning DOL prevailing wage thresholds
Candidate negotiates for signing bonus or equity without first maximizing base salary to the next wage level threshold

failure_patterns.pattern: Answering the salary history question reflexively before knowing whether it's legal to ask
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates treat recruiter questions as authoritative and feel social pressure to answer; disclosing feels cooperative while refusing feels adversarial
failure_patterns.consequence: Locks in a below-market anchor that the entire offer and negotiation is built around, often costing thousands to tens of thousands annually
warning_signs: You answered 'What are you currently making?' without pausing to consider whether you had to
You felt that refusing would 'hurt your chances' even in a state where the question was illegal

failure_patterns.pattern: Anchoring Canadian salary negotiation to US market data from levels.fyi or Glassdoor US
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Most widely available English-language salary content is US-centric; candidates assume it's globally applicable or don't know Canadian-specific sources exist
failure_patterns.consequence: Either anchoring 25–40% too high (seeming delusional to Canadian recruiters, losing offers) or using US data to validate accepting a below-market Canadian offer
warning_signs: Candidate cites levels.fyi numbers without specifying 'Canada' data
Candidate quotes USD figures when discussing CAD-denominated roles

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming a higher salary automatically means a higher wage level classification
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The link between salary and wage level seems intuitive but is legally incorrect — wage level is determined by job duties and SOC code, not pay rate alone
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidate negotiates a higher salary expecting more lottery entries, but the LCA is filed at the same wage level because duties did not change, resulting in no improvement in selection odds
warning_signs: Candidate has not consulted or asked the employer's immigration attorney about the wage level of the LCA
Candidate conflates 'I earn more than prevailing wage' with 'I am at a higher wage level'

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming the employer's headquarters location determines which state's employment law applies
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Most people think of their employer's location as the relevant legal jurisdiction; remote work has decoupled this assumption but not the mental model
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidates in ban states like New York or California interviewing with Texas or Florida companies waive protections they actually have
warning_signs: You work remotely but have never checked whether your state's laws apply to your out-of-state employer
You assumed no ban applied because the company is headquartered in a non-ban state

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating Robert Half Canada ranges as the ceiling rather than the floor for FAANG Canada negotiation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Robert Half ranges represent the broad Canadian market including non-tech employers; candidates don't realize FAANG Canada (Amazon, Google, Shopify) pays 20–40% above these ranges
failure_patterns.consequence: Underanchoring at major tech companies — e.g., targeting $138K CAD for a senior SWE role where Amazon Canada pays $145K–$170K base and Google Canada pays $155K–$185K
warning_signs: Candidate treats Robert Half midpoint as the target rather than the floor
Candidate doesn't distinguish between FAANG Canada and general market benchmarks

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to use the retention/lottery-risk argument when already on an approved H-1B
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates focus on their own risk (fear of rocking the boat, visa dependency) rather than recognizing the employer's now-quantifiable cost of replacing them under the weighted lottery
failure_patterns.consequence: Existing H-1B holders leave significant leverage unused in salary reviews, accepting below-market compensation when they have asymmetric retention power
warning_signs: Candidate says 'I can't negotiate aggressively because I depend on my employer for my visa'
Candidate does not frame the cost of their replacement in terms of lottery re-entry risk when asking for a raise

failure_patterns.pattern: Voluntarily disclosing salary history to 'get ahead of it' or appear transparent
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates conflate general transparency as a value with strategic disclosure; they believe sharing builds rapport and reduces friction
failure_patterns.consequence: Voluntarily disclosed salary is explicitly exempt from ban-state protections, and the number anchors the offer regardless of intent
warning_signs: You volunteered your current salary before being asked
You included compensation history on an application form even when it was optional

failure_patterns.pattern: Not asking about signing bonus because the base salary feels acceptable
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates conflate 'I'm happy with the base' with 'negotiation is complete'; don't know that signing bonus is expected to be requested at Canadian tech companies
failure_patterns.consequence: Leaving $5K–$20K+ in immediately vested compensation unclaimed simply by not asking
warning_signs: Candidate verbally accepts offer on the spot without asking about signing bonus
Candidate says 'I don't want to push my luck' after getting base adjusted slightly

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating the wage-weighted lottery as a done deal without monitoring for legal challenges
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Final rules feel permanent once published; candidates and employers may not track litigation that could result in injunctions before the effective date
failure_patterns.consequence: Career and salary decisions made around the wage-level system may be premature if the rule is enjoined before FY2027 registration
warning_signs: No mention of monitoring immigration litigation news between December 2025 and February 2026
Employer or candidate is making long-term hiring decisions based solely on the rule without a contingency plan

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to document a salary history ban violation in the moment
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates are focused on the interview itself and don't think about legal compliance in real time; documentation feels like an escalation they're not ready to commit to
failure_patterns.consequence: Without documentation, you cannot file a complaint, cannot establish the violation occurred, and lose the legal leverage the violation would have given you
warning_signs: You remember being asked about salary history in a ban state but took no notes
You didn't record the interviewer's name, date, or exact phrasing of the question

failure_patterns.pattern: Evaluating Canadian city offers on gross salary alone without adjusting for provincial tax differences
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Gross salary is the visible number; provincial tax rates require a separate calculation that candidates don't bother to do at decision time
failure_patterns.consequence: Systematically undervaluing Alberta offers (no provincial tax = 8–12% more take-home) and overvaluing equivalent gross salaries in Ontario or BC
warning_signs: Candidate declines Calgary offer because 'it's lower than Toronto' without doing tax-adjusted comparison
Candidate doesn't ask about provincial tax implications when comparing multi-city offers

failure_patterns.pattern: Sitting passively on a low salary anchor after early disclosure instead of reframing
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates believe that revisiting a disclosed number looks inconsistent or desperate; they hope the employer will disregard it or be generous anyway
failure_patterns.consequence: The anchor compounds — every step of the offer process (base, bonus targets, equity refresh) is calibrated against the disclosed number rather than market rate
warning_signs: You shared a low number early and haven't introduced market data or role-scope context since
You're waiting for the offer to 'see what they come back with' rather than proactively resetting expectations

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a Research Scientist / Vector Institute postdoc-adjacent role without understanding the compensation gap vs. industry
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Academic prestige and research affiliation make low-compensation roles feel like career investments; candidates don't calculate the $60K–$90K postdoc vs. $120K–$200K industry researcher gap
failure_patterns.consequence: Forgoing $30K–$110K annually relative to industry researcher roles at Vector-affiliated companies doing equivalent work
warning_signs: Candidate accepts 'research track' framing without asking whether the role has industry or academic compensation structure
Candidate doesn't compare Vector-affiliated company researcher comp vs. Vector Institute direct compensation

failure_patterns.pattern: PGWP holders negotiating as if they are employer-tied when they are not
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Conflation of the Canadian immigration system with the US H-1B model; students assume any work authorization creates employer leverage because that's the dominant narrative in international student communities
failure_patterns.consequence: Accepting below-market offers or failing to counter at all during the period of maximum mobility leverage — typically the first 1–2 years of Canadian employment
warning_signs: Candidate says 'I don't want to push too hard because I might need them for my PR'
Candidate has not researched their PGWP expiry date versus CEC eligibility timeline

failure_patterns.pattern: Not countering at all due to fear of offer withdrawal
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates overestimate withdrawal risk — the fear feels disproportionate because losing an offer feels catastrophic even though the statistical rate is only 6%
failure_patterns.consequence: Leaving an average of $27,000/year on the table — compounded over a career this is a significant wealth gap
warning_signs: Thinking 'I don't want to seem greedy'
Accepting the first offer without asking any questions about flexibility

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating internal promotion compensation after accepting the promotion
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: People feel grateful for being chosen and don't want to seem ungrateful or risk having the offer rescinded — they accept first, then try to negotiate
failure_patterns.consequence: Leverage is gone once the promotion is accepted; the company has achieved their goal and has little incentive to increase comp beyond what they already offered
warning_signs: Saying 'thank you so much, I'm excited — can we also talk about comp?' after verbally accepting
Feeling like raising comp would seem greedy after being promoted

failure_patterns.pattern: Stopping negotiation after the first company counter
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates experience relief when the company moves at all and interpret any upward movement as the ceiling, not understanding the typical three-round arc
failure_patterns.consequence: Leaves money on the table — often 5–15% of comp — because the candidate didn't realize the first company counter is typically only 40–60% movement toward the ask
warning_signs: You feel grateful rather than strategic after the first counter
You haven't yet attempted to shift levers like signing bonus or equity

failure_patterns.pattern: Giving a number first when asked for salary expectations pre-offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Social pressure in the moment makes silence or deflection feel rude; candidates assume they must answer the question directly
failure_patterns.consequence: You anchor the entire negotiation at or below your stated number — the company has no reason to offer more than what you said you expected
warning_signs: You feel obligated to answer every recruiter question directly
You give a range 'to seem flexible' before you have any offer

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating non-cash levers as afterthoughts rather than primary negotiation targets
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates fixate on base salary as the sole measure of offer quality, not recognizing that non-cash levers often have different, more flexible budget owners
failure_patterns.consequence: Leaving $15,000–$40,000 in total compensation value on the table that could have been captured without touching the salary band
warning_signs: Candidate accepts the offer after a single salary exchange without exploring other levers
Candidate only asks about salary and equity in their negotiation conversation

failure_patterns.pattern: Signing the clawback clause without reading the termination trigger language
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates are focused on the bonus amount, not the conditions. Clawback language is buried in employment agreements and rarely flagged by recruiters. People assume 'clawback = if you quit early' without verifying.
failure_patterns.consequence: Being laid off and simultaneously receiving a demand letter to repay tens of thousands of dollars — financially devastating and legally binding
warning_signs: Contract uses 'for any reason or no reason' language
No explicit mention of layoff or reduction in force exclusion anywhere in the agreement

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting the first offer out of fear that any counter will cost the sponsorship
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Visa dependency creates asymmetric loss aversion — the perceived downside of losing sponsorship feels catastrophic, overriding the upside calculus of negotiating; fear is calibrated to the wrong level of risk
failure_patterns.consequence: 10–30% systematic under-compensation relative to domestic peers; compounded over a career, this is hundreds of thousands of dollars in foregone earnings
warning_signs: Thinking 'I should just be grateful they're willing to sponsor me'
Accepting without asking any questions about comp flexibility

failure_patterns.pattern: Naming a specific salary number before the company has made an offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates interpret the question as a necessary formality or feel that providing a number demonstrates decisiveness and confidence
failure_patterns.consequence: Anchors the negotiation at the candidate's stated number rather than the company's ceiling; if the number is below what the company would have offered, the candidate has permanently reduced their own outcome
warning_signs: Feeling relieved to 'get the salary question out of the way' early
Treating the compensation question as a qualification screening step rather than a negotiation move

failure_patterns.pattern: Comparing offers by base salary only
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Base salary is the most visible and legible number; equity and bonus require calculation and ask-specific questions to quantify, so candidates default to the easily comparable figure
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidates accept offers that are $50,000-$100,000+ lower in actual annual compensation because the base salary appeared competitive
warning_signs: Saying 'both offers are about the same' without calculating annualized equity
Not knowing the bonus target percentage of either offer

failure_patterns.pattern: Delaying CEC Express Entry application until late in PGWP validity period
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Focus on job performance and unfamiliarity with immigration timelines; candidates assume there is more buffer than exists once processing times are factored in
failure_patterns.consequence: PR not granted before PGWP expiry, triggering actual employer dependency and LMIA need — turning an assumed weakness into a real one
warning_signs: Candidate is 18+ months into PGWP with NOC TEER 0/1 experience but has not started Express Entry profile
Candidate is unaware of current Express Entry processing times or CEC draw frequency

failure_patterns.pattern: Countering based on personal need rather than market data
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates frame their counter as 'I need more to pay rent/student loans' rather than anchoring to external market benchmarks
failure_patterns.consequence: Recruiter has an easy rebuttal since personal need is not their problem; data-anchored counters are structurally harder to dismiss
warning_signs: Using phrases like 'I was hoping for more'
Not pulling levels.fyi data before the negotiation conversation

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a retention counter-offer when the root cause was not compensation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Money is tangible and immediate; the real reasons for dissatisfaction (bad manager, no scope, stagnation) are harder to quantify and easier to temporarily rationalize away
failure_patterns.consequence: 80% of people who accept retention counter-offers leave within 12 months anyway — you've burned the external opportunity and damaged your internal relationship
warning_signs: Telling yourself 'the money makes it worth staying' while knowing the job itself hasn't changed
Feeling relief at the counter-offer without feeling excited about the work

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating without a BATNA
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates focus on what they want rather than what they'll do if they don't get it, treating the negotiation as a one-sided request rather than a bilateral decision
failure_patterns.consequence: Either accepts a package below their real floor, or overplays their hand with an arbitrary anchor and damages the offer
warning_signs: You haven't identified a specific walk-away number before the conversation
You're not sure whether you'd actually decline if the company doesn't move

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting or declining a verbal offer on the spot
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Emotional response to good news triggers immediate acceptance; or anxiety about seeming indecisive triggers quick response
failure_patterns.consequence: You lose the window to do market research and negotiate from a position of information rather than gratitude or panic
warning_signs: You say 'yes' or signal strong acceptance during the call where the offer is delivered
You ask no clarifying questions when the offer is presented

failure_patterns.pattern: Asking for everything at once in a single negotiation conversation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Fear that there will be no second opportunity to negotiate, leading candidates to front-load all asks to avoid missing anything
failure_patterns.consequence: Appears transactional and extraction-focused; reduces recruiter and hiring manager goodwill and willingness to advocate internally
warning_signs: Candidate drafts a list of 7+ items to negotiate before any conversation begins
Candidate frames the conversation as 'here are all the things I need' rather than 'here are the one or two things that matter most'

failure_patterns.pattern: Spending the signing bonus before the clawback period clears
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The bonus feels like income once it hits your account. People don't viscerally treat it as contingent. No one reminds you of the liability.
failure_patterns.consequence: When a clawback is triggered — especially via layoff — you must repay money you no longer have, creating debt and financial stress during unemployment
warning_signs: No mental or physical separation of the signing bonus from regular funds
Large purchases or debt paydown from signing bonus within the first 6 months

failure_patterns.pattern: Disclosing visa status before the company is invested in hiring you
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students conflate honesty with timing — believing transparency requires early disclosure, or they fear being 'caught' later if they wait
failure_patterns.consequence: Sponsorship cost becomes an elimination filter before qualifications are weighed, reducing interview opportunities unnecessarily
warning_signs: Mentioning OPT or H-1B need in a cover letter unprompted
Volunteering visa status in an initial phone screen before being asked

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting an offer on the spot during the verbal delivery call
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Excitement and relief override deliberate decision-making; candidates fear appearing ungrateful or difficult, and recruiters often imply that immediate acceptance is the expected response
failure_patterns.consequence: Signals that the candidate did not know negotiation was possible or expected; leaves money on the table across all negotiable dimensions without any attempt to improve terms
warning_signs: Saying 'Yes, absolutely!' before even hearing the full offer details
Not asking for the offer in writing before committing

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting startup equity valuations from recruiters at face value
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Recruiters present equity with optimistic future valuations that feel compelling; candidates lack the framework to apply stage-appropriate discounts
failure_patterns.consequence: Financial planning built on equity that never materializes, leading to compensation that is effectively just the base salary with no upside realized
warning_signs: Recruiter describes equity value using projected post-IPO or next-round valuations
Candidate cannot answer what the current 409A valuation is

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating all competing offers as equally usable leverage regardless of LMIA logistics
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates focus on the dollar value of a competing offer without assessing whether the competing employer can actually complete the work authorization transfer in a practical timeframe
failure_patterns.consequence: Competing offer leverage collapses when the current employer correctly points out that the competing offer requires a 3–5 month LMIA process — the bluff is called
warning_signs: Competing offer is from a company with no prior LMIA history and no GTS designation
Candidate has not verified LMIA processing pathway before using the offer in negotiation

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating all compensation components simultaneously in the first exchange
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates want to optimize total comp and bundle everything together, not realizing this reduces leverage on each individual component
failure_patterns.consequence: Recruiter can trade off components against each other; candidate ends up with less on each lever than if negotiated sequentially
warning_signs: Sending a counter that includes a new base, new equity, and new signing bonus all at once
Framing the ask as 'I need total comp of X' without separating components

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating a verbal promotion promise as binding without written criteria
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Employees trust their manager relationship and don't want to appear distrustful by asking for things in writing
failure_patterns.consequence: Promotions get delayed indefinitely, criteria shift, managers change — the employee has no accountability mechanism and loses months or years of career progression
warning_signs: Manager says 'you're on track' but can't specify what 'on track' means
Promotion timeline keeps slipping with new reasons each cycle

failure_patterns.pattern: Fabricating a competing offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates know competing offers are the strongest lever but don't have one, so they invent one to create urgency
failure_patterns.consequence: Recruiters verify offers; if caught, the offer is rescinded and professional trust is destroyed
warning_signs: You're tempted to reference a competing offer you don't actually have
You're unsure what details the company might ask to verify

failure_patterns.pattern: Folding after the first 'this is our best and final offer'
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The phrase sounds definitive and candidates interpret it as a true hard stop rather than a negotiating position
failure_patterns.consequence: You leave money on the table — signing bonus and other levers often remain available even when base is genuinely capped
warning_signs: You treat 'best and final' as equivalent to 'nothing else is possible'
You never ask about signing bonus after being told base cannot move

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting verbal commitments on remote work without written confirmation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates feel uncomfortable appearing distrustful by insisting on written terms, especially after a warm recruiter relationship has developed
failure_patterns.consequence: Remote arrangements evaporate after policy changes or manager transitions, with no contractual basis to object
warning_signs: Offer letter is silent on remote work arrangement
Recruiter says 'that's not something we typically put in writing' when asked to formalize remote terms

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming the clawback only applies if you voluntarily quit
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: That is true for well-written contracts. Many people assume the standard applies without checking if the actual language matches the assumption.
failure_patterns.consequence: Shock and financial liability after a layoff — the exact scenario where someone can least afford to repay a large lump sum
warning_signs: Never read the specific termination trigger language
Relied on recruiter verbal description of clawback terms instead of the contract

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating from personal financial need rather than market data
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students anchor to what they need to survive (student loan payments, living costs) rather than what the market pays, because personal need feels more concrete and urgent
failure_patterns.consequence: Reveals the negotiating floor to the employer, who can then anchor just above it — eliminating all upside from the range
warning_signs: Framing a counter as 'I need at least X because of my loans'
Not having looked up compensation data on levels.fyi or H-1B disclosure databases before negotiating

failure_patterns.pattern: Revealing current compensation when asked without redirecting
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates assume the question is standard and that refusing to answer will harm their candidacy; the social pressure to answer direct questions overrides strategic awareness
failure_patterns.consequence: Provides the company an anchor for your offer based on your past underpayment rather than your market value; particularly costly for candidates currently earning below market
warning_signs: Treating HR's request for current salary as a required form field
Not having a prepared deflection response before the first recruiter call

failure_patterns.pattern: Giving a number or accepting verbally on the first offer call
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates feel social pressure to respond positively in the moment; excitement or relief at receiving an offer overrides strategic patience
failure_patterns.consequence: Forfeits negotiating leverage before any counter has been made; the recruiter registers the candidate as satisfied at the initial number
warning_signs: Saying 'that sounds great' or 'I think I can work with that' on the first call
Not knowing what questions to ask about the offer components in the moment

failure_patterns.pattern: Answering 'Do you need sponsorship?' as 'Yes' when on PGWP
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates conflate long-term PR sponsorship needs with current work authorization requirements; they interpret the question as asking about their eventual immigration trajectory rather than their current legal work status
failure_patterns.consequence: Screened out of roles where they were fully eligible to work immediately, losing interview opportunities unnecessarily
warning_signs: Candidate does not have a prepared, accurate one-sentence description of their current work permit status
Candidate has checked 'Yes' to sponsorship questions on job applications while holding an active PGWP

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting 'base is fixed' without pivoting to signing bonus or equity
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates interpret 'base is fixed' as 'the entire offer is fixed' and disengage from negotiation prematurely
failure_patterns.consequence: Leaves signing bonus and equity upside on the table — both of which come from different budget pools and remain negotiable even when base is locked
warning_signs: Immediately accepting after hearing 'base is our final number'
Not asking whether signing bonus or equity are separately negotiable

failure_patterns.pattern: Not calculating the promo clock impact before accepting an internal transfer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The promo clock reset is not prominently disclosed during transfer conversations — employees focus on role scope and immediate comp, not multi-year promotion trajectory
failure_patterns.consequence: A seemingly neutral lateral move delays the next promotion by 2+ years, representing significant lost comp and seniority
warning_signs: Accepting a transfer at the same level without asking 'does this reset my promotion eligibility?'
Assuming the new team will count your prior tenure toward promotion

failure_patterns.pattern: Continuing to push after all three levers have been addressed
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates don't track how many components they've already negotiated and keep pushing without recognizing that the negotiation space is exhausted
failure_patterns.consequence: Signals extraction-maximizing behavior, damages goodwill, and can cause a company to rescind or reduce advocacy for the candidate
warning_signs: You've already moved on base, equity, and signing bonus
The recruiter has volunteered that they've gone back to the hiring manager multiple times

failure_patterns.pattern: Paralysis in the moment — knowing you should negotiate but not knowing the words
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates understand the principle but have no rehearsed scripts, so anxiety in the moment prevents execution
failure_patterns.consequence: Either no negotiation happens at all, or the ask is framed poorly and creates unnecessary friction without achieving movement
warning_signs: You have researched market data but still say nothing when the offer comes
You plan to negotiate 'if the number feels low' but have no script prepared

failure_patterns.pattern: Using signing bonus as the first negotiation ask instead of the fallback
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates perceive signing bonus as the 'safe' ask because it feels less confrontational than pushing on base salary
failure_patterns.consequence: Burning the most flexible lever early, before exhausting base salary and equity, and ending up with less total comp than a sequenced approach would have yielded
warning_signs: Candidate opens with 'Can you add a signing bonus?' before any salary discussion
Candidate hasn't researched the comp band to know whether base is actually at ceiling

failure_patterns.pattern: Not negotiating clawback terms because it feels awkward or risky to push back
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates fear that pushing back on clawback language signals distrust or intent to leave early. They don't know these terms are negotiable.
failure_patterns.consequence: Signing unfavorable terms that could cost thousands of dollars — leaving money and protection on the table that experienced candidates routinely secure
warning_signs: Accepted offer letter without any redline or question about clawback terms
Assumed the terms were standard and non-negotiable without asking

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting 'we'll figure out sponsorship' as a sufficient commitment before signing
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students are relieved to hear a positive sponsorship signal and don't want to seem demanding by pressing for specifics, especially after salary negotiation has already created perceived friction
failure_patterns.consequence: Onboarding into a company that lacks immigration infrastructure — no counsel, no prior H-1B experience — and facing a failed or delayed H-1B filing with status consequences
warning_signs: No written confirmation of H-1B filing intent in the offer documentation
Company cannot name their immigration attorney when asked

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating with visible frustration or declining enthusiasm when numbers disappoint
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Genuine emotional reaction to a low offer; candidates conflate 'negotiating hard' with 'expressing disappointment' as a pressure tactic
failure_patterns.consequence: Makes the candidate less attractive at precisely the moment leverage is most needed; companies de-prioritize candidates who seem likely to accept unhappily or leave quickly
warning_signs: Responding to a low offer with a long silence followed by a flat tone
Statements like 'I was hoping for significantly more than that'

failure_patterns.pattern: Fabricating or exaggerating a competing offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates know competing offers are powerful leverage but don't have one; they inflate a real offer or invent one to gain negotiating power
failure_patterns.consequence: If the recruiter asks for documentation or the fabrication is discovered, trust is destroyed and the offer may be rescinded; the tactic is explicitly flagged as something never to do
warning_signs: Citing a competing offer from a company whose process hasn't produced a written offer
Being unable to provide specifics when the recruiter asks follow-up questions about the competing offer

failure_patterns.pattern: Raising LMIA requirement with startups before receiving an offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Desire to avoid wasted effort or perceived transparency obligation; candidates disclose immigration needs in cover letters or early screening calls
failure_patterns.consequence: Screened out before demonstrating value; foregoes any chance of converting genuine technical interest into an offer that could then be negotiated
warning_signs: Candidate mentions visa status in cover letter or application form to companies without established immigration programs
Candidate asks about sponsorship policy in the first recruiter screen before receiving any signal of interest

failure_patterns.pattern: Using the initial offer as the anchor for the counter rather than market data
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The initial offer is salient and emotionally anchors the candidate, causing them to think in terms of percentage above what they were offered rather than what the market pays
failure_patterns.consequence: Counter lands below market rate even after negotiation, especially when the initial offer was significantly below median
warning_signs: Calculating counter as 'X% above what they offered' without checking levels.fyi
Not knowing the levels.fyi median before entering the negotiation

failure_patterns.pattern: Anchoring internal promotion negotiations on current salary rather than market rate for the new role
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Both employee and employer default to 'what you're making now plus a percentage' framing — it's the path of least resistance and feels fair
failure_patterns.consequence: Employee gets locked in below market for the new role level, and the underpayment compounds with each subsequent annual increase
warning_signs: Thinking 'a 10% raise seems reasonable for a promotion'
Not researching market comp for the new role before the conversation

failure_patterns.pattern: Misreading 'final offer' as always having room
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates learn that 'final offer' is often a negotiating tactic and apply that heuristic uniformly, even when the signal has shifted to genuinely final
failure_patterns.consequence: Pushes past the real ceiling, damages relationship, and occasionally triggers offer rescission
warning_signs: The recruiter's tone has shifted from sympathetic to matter-of-fact
A hard deadline has been attached to the final offer statement

failure_patterns.pattern: Conducting all negotiation over email when a phone call would be more effective
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Email feels safer, less confrontational, and gives candidates time to craft responses carefully
failure_patterns.consequence: Recruiters can batch-process and decline easily in writing; live advocacy and real-time movement almost never happen over email
warning_signs: You have never asked to move the negotiation to a phone call
You respond to offer details in the same email thread they were sent in

failure_patterns.pattern: Ignoring the tax impact of relocation packages
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates focus on the gross dollar amount of the relocation offer without understanding that it is taxable income, reducing net value by 25–40%
failure_patterns.consequence: Effective relocation support is significantly lower than expected, potentially leaving the candidate underresourced during a high-cost transition
warning_signs: Candidate accepts a flat relocation number without asking about tax treatment
Candidate doesn't request a gross-up to cover the tax liability

failure_patterns.pattern: Focusing only on the gross amount of the signing bonus, not the net liability
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Offer letters advertise the gross number. Taxes are invisible until you file. Most people don't calculate the repayment gap until they're actually asked to repay.
failure_patterns.consequence: Believing you owe $20K (what you kept) when you legally owe $30K (gross), creating an unexpected $10K shortfall
warning_signs: No discussion of gross vs. net in the signed agreement
Didn't ask or receive written confirmation that repayment is net-based

failure_patterns.pattern: Believing H-1B dependency means you cannot credibly imply you might leave
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students overestimate the legal and logistical complexity of H-1B transfer and underestimate their rights under portability rules, making employer leverage feel absolute when it is not
failure_patterns.consequence: Surrenders all implied BATNA power in negotiations, allowing employers to make take-it-or-leave-it offers without credible pushback
warning_signs: Not researching H-1B portability rules before entering a negotiation
Declining to explore competing offers because 'it's too complicated with my visa'

failure_patterns.pattern: Letting an exploding offer deadline lapse without explicitly requesting an extension
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Conflict-averse candidates assume that the company will proactively reach out or that their interest is self-evident; they also fear that challenging the deadline will signal wavering commitment
failure_patterns.consequence: Offer lapses; the candidate loses the option entirely when a single direct sentence would have extended the window in nearly every case
warning_signs: Thinking 'they must know I'm still interested' without having communicated it
Treating the deadline as a genuine signal about the company's culture rather than a standard pressure tactic

failure_patterns.pattern: Using Glassdoor or PayScale for tech compensation research
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: These platforms are widely known brand names for salary data; candidates don't realize they systematically mishandle equity and underreport tech compensation
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidates anchor their negotiation targets to artificially low benchmarks, leaving significant compensation on the table
warning_signs: Citing a salary range from Glassdoor that is 20-30% below levels.fyi data for the same role
Not knowing whether the cited salary figure includes equity

failure_patterns.pattern: Using an external offer as leverage without being genuinely prepared to take it
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: People generate an offer to gain negotiating power but haven't fully decided — they reveal the offer but fold when the company makes any counter, signaling they were bluffing
failure_patterns.consequence: Company learns you're a flight risk but not a credible one — future negotiations are weakened and you may be deprioritized
warning_signs: Getting an offer just to have 'something to show' without serious evaluation of taking it
Feeling relieved when the company counters so you don't have to decide

failure_patterns.pattern: Conflating sponsorship willingness with sponsorship execution capacity
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Both are binary 'yes/no' answers in conversation, making them feel equivalent — students don't know what questions to ask to distinguish intent from capability
failure_patterns.consequence: Accepting an offer from a company that wants to sponsor but cannot execute, resulting in a failed H-1B and potential status loss
warning_signs: Company has never sponsored an H-1B before but says they're willing to start
No current H-1B employees identifiable at the company

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating solely on salary and stopping when salary hits a ceiling
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates frame compensation mentally as 'salary' rather than 'total package'; when one number stops moving, they conclude negotiation is over
failure_patterns.consequence: Misses signing bonuses, equity grants, professional development budgets, extra vacation, flexible work arrangements — all of which the company may grant freely once salary is exhausted
warning_signs: Accepting 'our salary band is fixed' as the end of the conversation
Not having prepared a list of non-salary items before entering negotiation

failure_patterns.pattern: Using the final commitment close ('I'll sign today if you reach X') too early or insincerely
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The tactic sounds powerful and candidates deploy it as a negotiating probe rather than a genuine commitment
failure_patterns.consequence: Destroys credibility with the recruiter; if the number is met and the candidate still doesn't sign, the recruiter loses trust and future negotiations are compromised
warning_signs: Making the commitment close before having fully evaluated the offer
Using the phrase more than once in the same negotiation

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating negotiation as morally questionable or as 'haggling'
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Cultural conditioning, particularly among engineers, frames compensation discussion as unseemly; candidates internalize this as a virtue signal about being 'not money-motivated'
failure_patterns.consequence: Creates systematic and permanent undercompensation that compounds across raises, future offers, and decades of career earnings
warning_signs: Saying 'I don't want to seem greedy' when considering whether to counter
Feeling genuine discomfort or guilt when the recruiter pushes back on a counter-offer

failure_patterns.pattern: Using personal financial need rather than market data as the primary justification for a higher number
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates know their own expenses intimately and assume the employer will find them sympathetic; it feels honest and direct to explain personal circumstances
failure_patterns.consequence: Need-based justifications are weak because they're not connected to the candidate's labor value; they can also signal financial desperation, weakening leverage
warning_signs: Opening a counter with 'I have significant student loans' as the primary argument
Not having researched market compensation data before the negotiation call

failure_patterns.pattern: Accidentally implying the need for employer sponsorship when you actually hold an open work permit
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Cover letter or resume language is written generically without considering that Canadian employers may not know what PGWP means; phrases like 'work permit holder' or vague future references to PR processes trigger sponsorship assumptions
failure_patterns.consequence: Automatic rejection or recruiter disengagement before qualifications are reviewed — the original poster confirmed this happened to them despite being fully authorized to work
warning_signs: Cover letter mentions 'future visa needs' or 'immigration process' without explicitly clarifying no employer action is required
Resume lists work authorization status without specifying 'open work permit — any employer, no sponsorship'

failure_patterns.pattern: PGWP holders describing themselves as needing 'visa sponsorship' on job applications
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: International students absorb US-centric framing (OPT, H-1B sponsorship burden) from online communities and peer networks, then apply the same language to the fundamentally different Canadian PGWP context
failure_patterns.consequence: Employers who might otherwise hire freely filter out the candidate based on a perceived sponsorship burden that does not actually exist
warning_signs: Using the phrase 'I need sponsorship' in Canadian job applications as a PGWP holder
Checking 'yes' to sponsorship requirement questions when holding a PGWP

failure_patterns.pattern: Apologizing or over-hedging when disclosing visa status
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Anxiety about being perceived as a burden leads candidates to frame their status as a problem before the company has even assessed it as one
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidates come across worse than their actual visa situation warrants; signals lack of confidence to recruiters and hiring managers
warning_signs: Using phrases like 'I know this might be an issue but...'
Volunteering visa complexity before being asked in early screening stages

failure_patterns.pattern: Asking for a job in the first cold email
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The candidate's goal is a job, so they make that ask directly; they treat the email as a cover letter rather than as the opening move in a multi-step relationship
failure_patterns.consequence: Immediate close — the high-commitment ask triggers rejection before any relationship is established
warning_signs: Email includes phrases like 'I am interested in any open positions' or 'please consider me for a role'
The email attaches a resume in the first contact

failure_patterns.pattern: Optimizing advisor selection for h-index and publication record when the actual goal is an industry research job
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Academic prestige metrics are visible and legible; industry network strength is invisible and requires active investigation — so candidates default to what they can measure
failure_patterns.consequence: Graduating from a strong program with a well-cited advisor but no internship history at target companies, leading to weak positioning for industry research roles
warning_signs: Cannot name where the advisor's last 5 students interned
Advisor has no listed industry collaborations or visiting researcher roles on their faculty page

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting verbal H-1B sponsorship promises without written confirmation in the offer letter
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates feel it is awkward or risky to push back during offer negotiation, assume company reputation is sufficient guarantee, or don't know verbal promises are unenforceable
failure_patterns.consequence: When company policy changes, the employee has no legal recourse and faces abrupt status uncertainty mid-career, often with compressed time to find a new sponsor before the next cap season
warning_signs: Recruiter or manager says 'we sponsor H-1B' but offer letter contains no sponsorship language
Candidate feels relieved to get the offer and doesn't want to 'rock the boat' by asking for written confirmation

failure_patterns.pattern: Focusing exclusively on base salary when comparing offers, ignoring equity structure differences
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Base salary is concrete, immediate, and easy to compare; equity requires understanding vesting, strike prices, tax treatment, and liquidity — all of which feel uncertain and complex
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidates make regrettable decisions — choosing a slightly higher salary over meaningfully more valuable equity at a better-positioned company
warning_signs: Candidate says 'I just want a stable salary, the stock stuff is too complicated'
Candidate compares offers by base salary alone without modeling equity value scenarios
