diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If HR or recruiter: consider finding the relevant engineering or team manager on LinkedIn instead before sending

diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Which specific companies? Do they align with your target employers? Are placements recent (last 2-3 years) or historical?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Treat this as a strong signal that the advisor is not industry-connected regardless of their publication record; assess whether that fits your goals

diagnostic_questions.question: Is there any written documentation — offer letter, email, Slack message — that references H-1B sponsorship?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether any legal recourse (promissory estoppel) is viable and how strong that claim might be
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Consult an immigration attorney to assess whether the language is specific enough to support a promissory estoppel claim in your jurisdiction
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Treat the sponsorship promise as legally unenforceable and pivot immediately to finding a new sponsor — do not spend time on litigation

diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The financial and career math strongly favors skipping the PhD and entering industry directly

diagnostic_questions.question: How many months remain on your STEM OPT, and what is the deadline to have a new employer file for the next H-1B cap season?

diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the email reads as genuine targeted outreach or as a mass template blast, which determines whether it gets read or deleted
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If specific: strong signal; proceed
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If generic: revise the opening before sending; a generic compliment has the same effect as no compliment

diagnostic_questions.question: How long is the exercise window after leaving the company?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: A standard 90-day window creates enormous pressure and may force forfeiture of vested options if you cannot afford the strike price plus anticipated tax; longer windows are a meaningful benefit
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If 90 days: calculate whether you could afford to exercise all vested options if you left today
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If extended (2+ years or 10 years): this is a significant pro-employee benefit that reduces the lock-in effect of options

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a concrete sense of your market value from at least two independent data sources?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Without market data, any number you quote is a guess — and guesses tend to be either too low (leaving money on the table) or too high (ending negotiations prematurely).
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: you can state your expectation with confidence and justify it if challenged.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: do market research first — job boards, headhunters, or industry contacts — before entering the negotiation.

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you observed the promotion velocity of people currently in this role at this company?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the company's prestige advantage is real or offset by internal stagnation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If people are staying at the same level for 3-4 years, the prestige benefit may not outweigh the growth opportunity at a smaller but faster-moving company
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Research LinkedIn profiles of current and former employees in that role to assess typical tenure before promotion

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the equity grant in the form of RSUs, ISO options, or NQSO options?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The tax treatment differs materially: RSUs are taxed as ordinary income at vest; ISOs have AMT exposure but potential capital gains treatment; NQSOs are taxed as ordinary income at exercise on the spread
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If RSUs at a public company: model the withholding mechanism and plan for share-based tax withholding reducing the number of shares received
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If options at a private company: evaluate liquidity timeline, strike price relative to current 409A valuation, and exercise cost before accepting

diagnostic_questions.question: How well do you match the specific requirements of this role, honestly assessed?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: How much negotiating leverage you actually have — a high-match candidate is harder to replace, giving them more room to push
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If match is 80%+, negotiate assertively and invoke match quality as a reason for the premium
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If match is below 70%, prioritize getting the offer over maximizing the number; aggressive negotiation risks losing the offer to a better-matched candidate

diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Single reporting line is simpler; assess the specific manager's style and alignment with your work preferences

industry_realities.common_belief: Canada has a national pay transparency law similar to the US federal standard
industry_realities.actual_reality: There is no single national pay transparency law in Canada requiring salary disclosure in job postings. As of 2025–2026, only BC, Ontario (25+ employees), and PEI have enacted substantive pay transparency requirements; Alberta and Quebec have not
industry_realities.implication: Candidates and advisors must identify the specific province of the role before assuming any pay transparency obligation exists

industry_realities.common_belief: The wage level on an H-1B filing reflects how much the employer wants to pay
industry_realities.actual_reality: The DOL explicitly states that the wage level reflects job complexity and supervision — not total compensation. A Level IV classification requires the job to involve high complexity, advanced expertise, minimal supervision, and often instruction of others. The salary alone does not determine the level.
industry_realities.implication: Candidates cannot simply request a Level IV filing to increase lottery odds; the job duties must genuinely qualify under DOL's complexity criteria, and misclassification constitutes an LCA violation

industry_realities.common_belief: All Canadian employers must post salary ranges in job ads
industry_realities.actual_reality: BC requires it for all employers only from January 1, 2026 (previously phased by size); Ontario requires it only for employers with 25+ employees from January 1, 2026; PEI for 10+ employees; Alberta and Quebec have no equivalent enacted requirement
industry_realities.implication: Candidates applying before January 1, 2026 to mid-sized BC employers, or to small Ontario employers, may not see a posted range even in covered provinces

industry_realities.common_belief: The prevailing wage floor is fixed and stable year to year
industry_realities.actual_reality: DOL prevailing wage thresholds are updated annually when BLS updates OEWS data. The FLC Data Center is the authoritative real-time source; prior-year values may be incorrect.
industry_realities.implication: Candidates and employers must verify current thresholds at flcdatacenter.com before any LCA filing; relying on cached or year-old figures risks underpaying below the current prevailing wage

industry_realities.common_belief: BC and Ontario have the same pay transparency rules, including a salary history ban
industry_realities.actual_reality: BC has both a salary range posting requirement AND an explicit salary history ban. Ontario has only a salary range posting requirement; asking about previous pay remains legally permissible in Ontario under the Working for Workers Four Act, 2024
industry_realities.implication: Candidates in Ontario cannot legally refuse a salary history question on the grounds that it is prohibited — that protection exists only in BC

industry_realities.common_belief: Prevailing wage data is only useful to determine the minimum an employer must pay
industry_realities.actual_reality: The DOL OFLC Performance Data publicly discloses exact wages an employer has paid for specific H-1B filings by occupation, location, and wage level. This is employer-disclosed, not estimated data.
industry_realities.implication: Before salary negotiation, a candidate can look up what the same employer paid for comparable H-1B roles in the same city, creating an employer-specific data-backed negotiation anchor

industry_realities.common_belief: The salary range posted in a Canadian job ad represents the maximum the employer will pay
industry_realities.actual_reality: The source explicitly states that employers sometimes post ranges lower than their true budget; negotiating above the posted range is described as reasonable when justified with market data
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should treat the posted range as a floor for negotiation, not a ceiling, and use external market data sources (Robert Half Canada, Glassdoor CA, Levels.fyi Canada, Job Bank Canada) to support offers above the range

industry_realities.common_belief: The H-1B lottery is purely random and unaffected by salary
industry_realities.actual_reality: Effective February 27, 2026, under Federal Register 2025-23853, the lottery is wage-weighted: Level I = 1 entry, Level II = 2 entries, Level III = 3 entries, Level IV = 4 entries. NFAP analysis indicates Level IV selection probability increases by 107% vs. the old random lottery.
industry_realities.implication: For cap-subject H-1B filings on or after February 27, 2026, negotiating a salary that crosses the Level III to Level IV threshold has dual impact: higher compensation AND a 33% relative increase in lottery entries

industry_realities.common_belief: Government of Canada Job Bank wage data reflects total compensation for tech roles
industry_realities.actual_reality: Job Bank Canada uses Statistics Canada Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (SEPH) data and captures base salary; the source explicitly states it may undercount total compensation including bonuses and equity
industry_realities.implication: Candidates benchmarking against Job Bank data alone may undervalue their total compensation target in roles where equity and bonuses are significant components

industry_realities.common_belief: PERM green card sponsorship is a reliable long-term path for all foreign nationals
industry_realities.actual_reality: For PERM, the offered wage must meet the prevailing wage at the time of PERM filing AND at the time the worker receives the visa. For Indian nationals in EB-2, current estimates place the wait at 134+ years, making PERM a theoretical rather than practical path.
industry_realities.implication: Indian nationals in EB-2 PERM pipelines should not rely on PERM as an actionable green card path under current backlog conditions

industry_realities.common_belief: Quebec's pay equity legislation functions as a pay transparency law for job postings
industry_realities.actual_reality: Quebec's Act Respecting Pay Equity is focused on gender pay equity between job groups for existing workers — it is not a job posting transparency requirement comparable to BC or Ontario's legislation
industry_realities.implication: Candidates applying to Quebec-based roles cannot use Quebec's pay equity law to require or expect a salary range in a job posting

industry_realities.common_belief: The federal Pay Equity Act (2021) requires all Canadian employers to disclose salary ranges in job postings
industry_realities.actual_reality: The federal Pay Equity Act (2021) applies only to federally regulated employers (Crown corporations, banks, telecommunications, interprovincial transportation) and is focused on gender pay equity between job groups — not individual job posting salary disclosure
industry_realities.implication: Candidates at federally regulated employers cannot invoke the federal Pay Equity Act to require a posted salary range

industry_realities.common_belief: H-1B candidates are in a weak negotiating position because they depend on employer sponsorship
industry_realities.actual_reality: Under the wage-weighted lottery, employers who have already sponsored an H-1B at Level III or IV face a quantifiable and asymmetric cost to replacing that employee — they must re-enter a lottery where there is a 50%+ chance of not getting selected at all
industry_realities.implication: Existing H-1B holders at Level III/IV have stronger retention leverage than most realize and should frame salary negotiations around the employer's lottery re-entry risk, not their own visa dependency

industry_realities.common_belief: If a recruiter asks you about your current salary, you are obligated to answer
industry_realities.actual_reality: In 22 states and 23+ municipalities, asking the question is illegal — the recruiter may not even know this, and candidates have the legal right to decline
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should know their state's status before any interview begins, and have a rehearsed redirect ready that doesn't create friction

industry_realities.common_belief: Salary negotiation advice and benchmarks are globally applicable — the same tactics and numbers work everywhere
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian tech salaries are 25–40% lower in USD terms than US equivalents, and the compensation structure is fundamentally different (base-heavy, less equity, narrower negotiating bands). US-calibrated advice actively misleads Canadian job seekers.
industry_realities.implication: Always source Canadian-specific benchmarks (Robert Half Canada, Glassdoor CA) before any Canadian negotiation — treat US data as a separate market entirely

industry_realities.common_belief: Salary negotiation for H-1B candidates is the same as for US citizens — maximize total comp using market data
industry_realities.actual_reality: Each salary dollar has asymmetric value for H-1B candidates if it crosses a wage level threshold, because it simultaneously increases purchasing power and lottery selection probability — a dual return unavailable to US citizens
industry_realities.implication: H-1B candidates should prioritize closing the gap to the next wage level threshold above other comp components (signing bonus, equity) when near a boundary, and should always negotiate with DOL prevailing wage data in hand

industry_realities.common_belief: Laws about salary history only apply to employers headquartered in that state
industry_realities.actual_reality: Protections follow the employee's physical location — Colorado explicitly covers out-of-state companies with Colorado-based employees; California applies to remote workers located in California
industry_realities.implication: Remote workers in ban states are protected even when their employer is in Texas, Florida, or any other non-ban state

industry_realities.common_belief: When a Canadian employer says 'the band is set,' negotiation is over
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian employers typically have less flexibility on base salary (3–10% negotiating band) but retain meaningful discretion on signing bonuses, which are expected to be asked for at tech companies
industry_realities.implication: When base is closed, immediately pivot to asking for a signing bonus rather than accepting the conversation as finished

industry_realities.common_belief: A higher salary means you will be classified at a higher wage level for H-1B purposes
industry_realities.actual_reality: Wage level is determined by the DOL's assessment of job duties against the SOC code definition — salary alone does not determine wage level. An employer can pay above prevailing wage while still filing at Level I if the duties match Level I
industry_realities.implication: Candidates must confirm both the salary and the duties-based wage level classification with immigration counsel; negotiating salary without confirming the LCA wage level may produce no improvement in lottery odds

industry_realities.common_belief: Pay transparency laws (posting salary ranges) primarily benefit employers by setting expectations
industry_realities.actual_reality: They structurally shift negotiating power to candidates by revealing the employer's actual budget before any negotiation begins
industry_realities.implication: In states with posting requirements, candidates should always anchor to the top of the posted range with justification rather than guessing or anchoring low

industry_realities.common_belief: Robert Half Canada salary ranges represent the ceiling for what you can negotiate
industry_realities.actual_reality: Robert Half ranges represent the broad market including non-tech employers. FAANG Canada (Amazon, Google, Shopify) pays 20–40% above Robert Half ranges, with senior SWE total comp reaching $175K–$260K+ CAD
industry_realities.implication: Use Robert Half as a floor benchmark to avoid being underpaid, but calibrate upward to FAANG Canada-specific data when negotiating with major tech employers

industry_realities.common_belief: The H-1B lottery is random and salary is irrelevant to selection odds
industry_realities.actual_reality: As of the FY2027 lottery (registration March 2026), the system is wage-weighted: Level IV applicants have 4 entries vs. Level I's 1 entry, more than doubling selection probability at the high end and halving it at the low end
industry_realities.implication: Any career or salary advice for H-1B candidates that does not account for the wage-weighted lottery is materially incomplete as of early 2026; wage level optimization is now a core component of H-1B career strategy

industry_realities.common_belief: Voluntarily sharing your salary is protected the same way as being asked for it in a ban state
industry_realities.actual_reality: Voluntary disclosure is explicitly carved out as an exception in virtually all salary history ban laws — once you share it unprompted, the legal protection no longer applies to that information
industry_realities.implication: Never volunteer salary information before an offer, even in casual conversation or to 'set expectations' — the legal protection disappears the moment you bring it up first

industry_realities.common_belief: A higher gross salary in Toronto always means more money than a lower gross salary in Calgary
industry_realities.actual_reality: Alberta has no provincial income tax, so a Calgary gross salary yields approximately 8–12% more take-home than the same gross in Ontario or BC
industry_realities.implication: Always compute after-tax take-home when comparing multi-city Canadian offers — do not compare gross salary figures across provinces without adjusting for provincial tax

industry_realities.common_belief: The wage-weighted lottery rule is a proposed regulation that may or may not pass
industry_realities.actual_reality: The rule was finalized on December 23, 2025 (Federal Register document 2025-23853) and takes effect February 27, 2026 — it is settled law as of early 2026, not a proposal
industry_realities.implication: Advisors, career coaches, and candidates referencing this as 'proposed' or 'pending' are operating on outdated information; decisions should be made as if the rule is in effect unless a court injunction is issued

industry_realities.common_belief: If an employer violates a salary history ban, there's nothing practical you can do
industry_realities.actual_reality: Six states (California, Colorado, Illinois, Massachusetts, New York, Washington) grant private rights to sue with remedies including back pay, wage differentials, attorney's fees, and civil penalties up to $25,000
industry_realities.implication: Documenting a violation in these states creates real legal leverage — not just a complaint mechanism — that can be carefully referenced in negotiation

industry_realities.common_belief: The Canada–US compensation gap is modest and mainly affects senior roles
industry_realities.actual_reality: For early/mid career in non-FAANG US, the gap is 20–40% and meaningful but not catastrophic. For FAANG: a senior SWE earns $150K–$220K CAD ($110K–$161K USD) in Canada vs. $250K–$400K USD at US FAANG — a gap that compounds severely over a career
industry_realities.implication: The decision to pursue a Canadian vs. US career path is a high-stakes financial decision that should be made with full awareness of the FAANG-level gap; immigration stability is a real but quantifiable offset

industry_realities.common_belief: Michigan and Wisconsin just don't have salary history bans, like most states
industry_realities.actual_reality: Michigan and Wisconsin have laws that actively prohibit local governments from passing salary history bans — even municipalities cannot protect workers there
industry_realities.implication: Workers in these states have zero salary history protection at any level of government; full compensation history disclosure can be legally required

industry_realities.common_belief: A Vector Institute research role and an industry researcher role at a Vector-affiliated company are comparable in compensation
industry_realities.actual_reality: Vector Institute direct (academic/postdoc-adjacent) pays $60K–$90K CAD. Industry researcher roles at Vector-affiliated companies pay $120K–$200K CAD — a gap of $30K–$110K+ annually for potentially equivalent work
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should explicitly clarify whether a research role has academic or industry compensation structure before accepting; the affiliation name alone does not determine pay level

industry_realities.common_belief: Statistics Canada data is the most reliable source for tech salary benchmarks
industry_realities.actual_reality: Statistics Canada SEPH data is based on payroll records and systematically undercounts tech compensation. Robert Half Canada and Glassdoor CA are more accurate for individual negotiation benchmarks.
industry_realities.implication: Do not use Statistics Canada SEPH as your primary negotiation reference; use it only for occupational trend analysis and rely on Robert Half Canada and Glassdoor CA for actual benchmarks

industry_realities.common_belief: Pay transparency laws don't matter until they're fully in force
industry_realities.actual_reality: BC and Ontario pay transparency legislation (effective Jan 2026 for Ontario employers with 25+ employees) will require posted salary ranges, eliminating information asymmetry that currently disadvantages candidates
industry_realities.implication: Early-complying employers already post ranges; candidates should ask for the salary band directly even before legislation takes full effect, since many employers will now share it

industry_realities.common_belief: International students in Canada always need employer sponsorship and therefore have reduced negotiation power
industry_realities.actual_reality: PGWP holders have an open work permit giving them identical mobility to Canadian citizens during the permit's validity — there is no employer-tied immigration dependency unless the candidate allows themselves to approach expiry without PR
industry_realities.implication: PGWP holders should negotiate with full leverage from day one, treating immigration status as irrelevant to the negotiation rather than as a concession they must make

industry_realities.common_belief: Asking for more after receiving an offer risks getting the offer pulled
industry_realities.actual_reality: Only 6% of offers are withdrawn after a counter — employers expect negotiation and withdrawal is almost exclusively reserved for candidates who are aggressive or disrespectful in tone, not those who simply ask for more
industry_realities.implication: The fear of withdrawal is statistically unjustified and should not be the reason you don't counter — the expected value of countering is strongly positive

industry_realities.common_belief: Internal promotions are fairly compensated because the company knows your value
industry_realities.actual_reality: Internal hires are systematically offered below market on the assumption they're 'already being paid' — the company anchors on your current salary plus an increment rather than market rate for the new role
industry_realities.implication: Always research and anchor on market comp for the new role level, not a percentage increase on current salary

industry_realities.common_belief: Salary negotiation is a single conversation where you make one ask
industry_realities.actual_reality: Negotiation is a structured multi-round process with a predictable arc; the first counter is rarely the final one, and companies expect at least one or two rounds
industry_realities.implication: Candidates who stop after the first company counter routinely leave money on the table because they don't understand the expected arc

industry_realities.common_belief: Exploding offer deadlines are firm and non-negotiable
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most exploding offer deadlines are negotiable — companies have invested 10–20 hours interviewing a candidate and will not lose them over a 3–7 day extension
industry_realities.implication: Always request an extension framed around making a confident decision; treat the deadline as a starting position, not a hard constraint

industry_realities.common_belief: If the salary is fixed or at the top of the band, there's nothing left to negotiate
industry_realities.actual_reality: Non-cash levers like signing bonus, PTO, remote work, pro dev budget, and title are often owned by different budget holders than base salary and remain fully negotiable even when base is at ceiling
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should treat a salary ceiling as the trigger to pivot to non-cash levers, not as the end of negotiation

industry_realities.common_belief: Clawback clauses only apply if you voluntarily quit — if you're laid off, you don't owe anything back
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many contracts — especially those written sloppily or aggressively — include 'for any reason or no reason' language that makes clawbacks applicable even after a layoff. The default assumption is wrong and legally dangerous.
industry_realities.implication: Never assume layoffs are excluded. Read the exact termination trigger language and negotiate explicit exclusions before signing.

industry_realities.common_belief: Sponsoring H-1B is expensive and justifies paying an international candidate below market
industry_realities.actual_reality: H-1B sponsorship costs $3,000–$8,000/year in attorney and USCIS fees — less than 5% of a $150,000+ employee's total cost. It is not a meaningful financial justification for 20% below-market compensation.
industry_realities.implication: When an employer uses sponsorship cost as a reason to offer less, it is a negotiation tactic, not a financial reality. Counter with the actual cost figures.

industry_realities.common_belief: Negotiating a job offer is rude, risky, or signals that you only care about money
industry_realities.actual_reality: Experienced hiring managers expect negotiation; candidates who accept immediately are often perceived as either inexperienced or unaware of their market value — both of which are competence signals that work against you
industry_realities.implication: Always counter at least once, framed positively; negotiation signals professional sophistication, not greed

industry_realities.common_belief: Glassdoor and PayScale give you accurate salary benchmarks for tech roles
industry_realities.actual_reality: These platforms wildly mishandle equity compensation and systematically underreport total comp for tech; levels.fyi and H-1B filings are the authoritative sources for tech compensation
industry_realities.implication: Candidates who benchmark using Glassdoor anchor their negotiations too low and leave significant money on the table; switch to levels.fyi before any negotiation

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian employers face the same LMIA burden as US employers face with H-1B, creating equivalent premium justification
industry_realities.actual_reality: Unlike H-1B, LMIA in Canada does not create ongoing employer lock-in for most international students who will transition through CEC Express Entry; the retention leverage argument is much weaker in Canada
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should not expect LMIA costs to generate automatic salary premiums in new job negotiations; the argument has force only in existing employer retention conversations

industry_realities.common_belief: When a company says 'base is our final number,' the entire negotiation is over
industry_realities.actual_reality: Signing bonuses come from a different budget than base salary headcount and are almost always still negotiable even after base is declared final
industry_realities.implication: Always pivot to signing bonus when base is locked — $20K–$80K in signing bonus is standard at large tech companies for senior roles and does not require reopening base

industry_realities.common_belief: A retention counter-offer means the company truly values you and wants you to stay
industry_realities.actual_reality: Companies often make retention counter-offers knowing the employee will probably leave anyway — it buys 6–12 months to find a replacement while the employee feels valued
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate a retention offer on whether it fixes the root cause of dissatisfaction, not on the emotional signal of being wanted

industry_realities.common_belief: 'Final offer' means the negotiation is over
industry_realities.actual_reality: The phrase 'final offer' is often a negotiating position, not a hard limit; the signal's meaning depends on delivery channel, tone, and whether a hard deadline is attached
industry_realities.implication: Assess context before taking 'final offer' at face value — an emailed 'final offer' from a sympathetic recruiter is different from the same phrase with a deadline on a phone call

industry_realities.common_belief: 'This is our best and final offer' means there is nothing left to negotiate
industry_realities.actual_reality: Base salary band may genuinely be locked, but signing bonus often comes from a completely different budget and may still have flexibility even after 'best and final'
industry_realities.implication: After hearing 'best and final,' pivot specifically to signing bonus before accepting or walking away

industry_realities.common_belief: PTO negotiation costs the company real money, so they're unlikely to flex on it
industry_realities.actual_reality: PTO doesn't cost the company direct cash — it costs coverage capacity — and adjustments typically don't require HR committee approval or trigger salary band reviews
industry_realities.implication: PTO is often one of the easiest levers to move because the approval path is short and the cash cost is indirect; it should be a standard ask

industry_realities.common_belief: If you trigger a clawback, you repay what you received
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most clawback clauses require repayment of the gross amount — the pre-tax figure. You may have only kept 67% of the bonus after taxes but owe 100% back, meaning you repay money you no longer have.
industry_realities.implication: Always confirm gross vs. net repayment terms in writing, and negotiate net-only repayment before signing.

industry_realities.common_belief: Pushing back on an offer as an international student risks having it rescinded, especially with sponsorship at stake
industry_realities.actual_reality: Offers are almost never rescinded for reasonable negotiation — companies have invested too much in the hiring process to withdraw over a counter. The fear of rescission is systematically miscalibrated.
industry_realities.implication: International students should negotiate with the same assertiveness as domestic candidates. The sponsorship relationship is not made fragile by a salary counter; it is made fragile by poor performance or bad cultural fit.

industry_realities.common_belief: A salary increase of a few thousand dollars isn't worth the awkwardness of negotiating
industry_realities.actual_reality: A $5,000 salary increase compounded over 10 years is worth approximately $100,000 gross; it also sets the baseline for every future raise and the anchor for your next employer's offer
industry_realities.implication: Calculate the true long-term value before deciding a request is too small to make; the compounding effect makes early-career negotiations disproportionately important

industry_realities.common_belief: Salary is the most important and negotiable component of an offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: Equity is often 30-60% of total comp at large tech companies; signing bonuses are one-time and the easiest component for companies to approve; base salary is often the most constrained by band limits
industry_realities.implication: When base is capped, shift negotiation focus to signing bonus and equity refresh rather than continuing to push on base

industry_realities.common_belief: Any LMIA-backed competing offer provides usable negotiation leverage
industry_realities.actual_reality: A competing offer requiring 2–5 months of standard LMIA processing is practically unusable as immediate leverage; employers know this and will not feel threatened by an offer you cannot realistically take for months
industry_realities.implication: Candidates needing LMIA sponsorship should specifically target GTS-approved employers for competing offers, since only these create practically credible walk-away alternatives

industry_realities.common_belief: Accepting a retention counter-offer from your current employer solves the problem
industry_realities.actual_reality: 80% of people who accept counter-offers leave within 12 months anyway because the underlying non-compensation reasons for considering leaving remain unresolved
industry_realities.implication: Before accepting a retention counter-offer, explicitly assess whether the reason you considered leaving was purely financial — if not, the counter-offer is a temporary fix

industry_realities.common_belief: An internal transfer to an interesting new role is a lateral move with no real cost
industry_realities.actual_reality: Internal transfers typically reset the promotion eligibility clock, meaning a mid-cycle transfer can delay your next promotion by 2+ years while also reducing institutional knowledge capital on your current team
industry_realities.implication: Always calculate the full promo clock and equity/bonus impact before accepting a transfer, and negotiate comp increases at the time of transfer

industry_realities.common_belief: You need to name the competing company to make a competing offer credible
industry_realities.actual_reality: You only need to share the number; companies don't require — and recruiters don't always verify — the specific employer
industry_realities.implication: Share the dollar amount but withhold the company name to avoid unnecessary comparison and maintain negotiating simplicity

industry_realities.common_belief: Negotiating aggressively will make you seem difficult and cost you the offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: Enthusiastic, specific, collaborative counter-offers are expected by recruiters — the scripts that work are not adversarial; they are good-faith conversations
industry_realities.implication: Tone and framing matter more than the act of negotiating — enthusiasm before any ask is not a tactic, it is what makes the ask land well

industry_realities.common_belief: A verbal commitment from a hiring manager or recruiter on remote work is reliable
industry_realities.actual_reality: Verbal agreements on remote work have no enforcement mechanism; manager changes, policy shifts, or return-to-office mandates can nullify them with no recourse for the employee
industry_realities.implication: Remote work terms must appear explicitly in the offer letter with precise language; anything short of that is not a secured benefit

industry_realities.common_belief: Clawback terms are non-negotiable boilerplate — you can't push back on them
industry_realities.actual_reality: All four major clawback terms — structure, period length, gross/net, and termination triggers — are negotiable. Reputable companies will engage on these. A refusal to negotiate any of them is itself informative.
industry_realities.implication: Always attempt to negotiate clawback terms as a standard part of offer negotiation, not an exceptional ask.

industry_realities.common_belief: H-1B holders are legally locked in to their employer and cannot credibly threaten to leave
industry_realities.actual_reality: H-1B portability rules allow you to switch employers without waiting for approval, as long as the new petition is filed within 60 days of the switch. You are not trapped.
industry_realities.implication: Knowing and internalizing portability rights converts a perceived permanent constraint into a manageable one — and makes competing offer leverage genuinely credible for H-1B holders.

industry_realities.common_belief: The company is doing you a favor by hiring you
industry_realities.actual_reality: By the time an offer is extended, the company has already invested tens of thousands of dollars in interviewing you and has decided they need you to solve a specific business problem; they are highly motivated not to lose you
industry_realities.implication: Enter negotiation understanding that you have substantial leverage — the company wants to close this deal as much as you do

industry_realities.common_belief: Recruiters will volunteer all relevant compensation details when making an offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: Critical details like the option exercise window, fully diluted ownership percentage, liquidation preferences, and 409A valuations are almost never volunteered; they must be explicitly asked for
industry_realities.implication: Candidates must run a structured checklist of equity questions on every offer call or risk agreeing to terms that significantly reduce actual compensation value

industry_realities.common_belief: Checking 'Yes' to the sponsorship question on Canadian job applications is required honesty for PGWP holders
industry_realities.actual_reality: PGWP is an open work permit; the accurate and legally correct answer is that no LMIA or employer sponsorship is required for current work authorization
industry_realities.implication: PGWP holders should answer sponsorship questions as 'No' or clarify 'I hold an open work permit and do not require employer-specific sponsorship,' avoiding unnecessary screening-out from roles they are legally eligible to take immediately

industry_realities.common_belief: The right counter is a percentage above what the company offered
industry_realities.actual_reality: The right counter is anchored to market data (levels.fyi median for the specific company, level, and location), not to the initial offer — using the initial offer as your anchor can result in landing below market even after negotiation
industry_realities.implication: Always pull levels.fyi before building your counter number and start from market, not from the offer

industry_realities.common_belief: You need to wait for the annual review cycle to address a comp gap
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most companies have off-cycle market correction mechanisms that are almost never proactively offered — they exist but require the employee to explicitly request them with documented market data
industry_realities.implication: If you have clear evidence of a 15–20%+ comp gap and strong performance, don't wait for annual review — request a market correction conversation explicitly

industry_realities.common_belief: Once you've signed an offer, negotiation is over
industry_realities.actual_reality: Post-acceptance negotiation is possible at 90-day reviews, when scope expands, or when market rates shift materially — but requires strong performance as the foundation
industry_realities.implication: Candidates who underestimate their value at signing can recover ground post-hire if they build a track record quickly and frame the ask around market data and delivered scope

industry_realities.common_belief: Email is a professional and effective channel for salary negotiation
industry_realities.actual_reality: Recruiters can batch and decline email negotiations with minimal friction — live phone calls are where real advocacy and movement happen
industry_realities.implication: Proactively request a phone call before submitting any counter-offer, even if the entire process has been conducted via email

industry_realities.common_belief: An inflated title at a startup is a career asset because it looks impressive
industry_realities.actual_reality: Large tech employers benchmark candidates against the scope expectations of that title level; an inflated title that doesn't match your actual scope can cause downleveling and comp suppression at the next role
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate title upgrades at startups against how they will be interpreted by your next employer, not just how they sound

industry_realities.common_belief: Clawback enforcement is aggressive — companies always pursue full repayment through courts
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most clawback enforcement happens through the offboarding process via withheld final paychecks or formal demand letters. Court action is rare unless amounts are very large. Companies and employees often negotiate the actual amount informally even after a clawback is triggered.
industry_realities.implication: If a clawback is triggered and you have a legitimate grievance, negotiating the amount after the fact is a real option — don't assume the stated amount is the final outcome.

industry_realities.common_belief: Visa status is purely a negotiating liability — it makes you a more expensive, riskier hire
industry_realities.actual_reality: Visa holders have a demonstrable retention advantage — they are significantly less likely to job-hop due to immigration switching costs, meaning employers get a longer-tenure employee for the same investment
industry_realities.implication: Visa holders should explicitly surface retention value as a counter-narrative to the cost framing, reorienting the conversation from 'I cost more because of sponsorship' to 'I stay longer and that has real value.'

industry_realities.common_belief: If you ask for more than they can give, they'll rescind the offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: The absolute worst realistic outcome of a reasonable counter-offer is receiving the original offer unchanged; companies do not rescind offers because candidates negotiated in good faith
industry_realities.implication: The asymmetry of outcomes (upside: more money; downside: original offer) makes negotiating always the correct expected-value decision

industry_realities.common_belief: Asking for more will make you seem greedy and risk the offer being rescinded
industry_realities.actual_reality: People who negotiate get an average 18.83% more than those who accept the first offer; offers are almost never rescinded for polite, well-framed negotiation
industry_realities.implication: The expected value of negotiating is highly positive and the downside risk is near zero when done with warmth and professionalism

industry_realities.common_belief: Bridging open work permits provide the same mobility as a PGWP
industry_realities.actual_reality: Some bridging open work permits are tied to the original sponsoring employer; leaving that employer may invalidate work authorization even if the permit category sounds open
industry_realities.implication: Candidates in PR application processes should verify the specific conditions of their bridging permit before assuming they have the same walk-away leverage as PGWP holders

industry_realities.common_belief: You need to disclose the competing company's name to use a competing offer as leverage
industry_realities.actual_reality: The competing offer number is the leverage — you are not required to disclose the company name and doing so adds no benefit while potentially creating complications
industry_realities.implication: When using a competing offer, share the number but decline to name the company if uncomfortable doing so

industry_realities.common_belief: Telling your employer you have an external offer gives you leverage with no downside if you stay
industry_realities.actual_reality: Revealing that you're considering leaving permanently changes the relationship — even if you stay via counter-offer, you're now flagged as a flight risk and may be quietly deprioritized for promotions or key assignments
industry_realities.implication: Only use an external offer as internal leverage if you are genuinely prepared to take it — treat revealing it as a one-way door

industry_realities.common_belief: Companies have a fixed budget and all levers are equally constrained
industry_realities.actual_reality: Different comp components — base, signing bonus, equity — come from different budget pools with different levels of flexibility; base may be at ceiling while signing bonus has room
industry_realities.implication: When one lever is locked, shift to another rather than treating the whole package as immovable

industry_realities.common_belief: Giving a salary range signals flexibility and makes you easier to work with
industry_realities.actual_reality: Ranges anchor at the low end — the company treats the bottom of your range as your actual ask and has no incentive to offer more
industry_realities.implication: Always give one specific number when counter-offering, never a range

industry_realities.common_belief: Negotiating multiple things at once is more efficient and shows you know what you want
industry_realities.actual_reality: Presenting a long list of asks signals extraction-maximizing behavior and reduces recruiter and hiring manager willingness to advocate internally on your behalf
industry_realities.implication: Prioritize to 2–3 levers with specific rationale; sequential, targeted asks produce better outcomes than comprehensive lists

industry_realities.common_belief: A signing bonus is equivalent to extra salary — just paid upfront
industry_realities.actual_reality: A signing bonus carries clawback contingency that salary does not. It is better understood as a conditional advance that becomes yours only after the clawback period clears.
industry_realities.implication: Do not spend signing bonus funds as if they are unconditional income until the clawback period has passed.

industry_realities.common_belief: If a company says they will sponsor H-1B, the immigration component of the offer is settled
industry_realities.actual_reality: Sponsorship willingness and execution capacity are entirely different things. A company without immigration counsel, prior H-1B filings, or current H-1B employees may be genuinely willing but structurally unable to deliver.
industry_realities.implication: Verify execution infrastructure — not just intent — before signing. Ask about immigration counsel, prior H-1B history, and current H-1B employees as due diligence items equivalent to verifying salary.

industry_realities.common_belief: The salary the company offers reflects what the market says you're worth
industry_realities.actual_reality: First offers reflect the company's budget target and what they think they can get away with based on information they have about you; it is not a market clearing price
industry_realities.implication: Treat the first offer as the opening position in a negotiation, not as a take-it-or-leave-it assessment of your value

industry_realities.common_belief: A competing offer from a company you wouldn't actually take is just as useful as a real one
industry_realities.actual_reality: Fabricating or exaggerating competing offers is explicitly flagged as something to never do; the tactic only works when genuine and can destroy the offer if discovered
industry_realities.implication: Only cite competing offers that are real, documented, and from companies you would actually consider; the leverage comes from credibility, not the existence of a number

industry_realities.common_belief: 'Sponsorship' means the same thing to all Canadian employers asking the question
industry_realities.actual_reality: The question is ambiguous in Canada — it may mean LMIA specifically, or any work permit assistance at all; the interpretation varies by employer and HR sophistication
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should proactively clarify their current status ('I hold an open work permit') rather than answering a binary yes/no, which avoids both dishonesty and unnecessary self-disqualification

industry_realities.common_belief: Negotiating hard signals you are difficult to work with
industry_realities.actual_reality: 66% of candidates who negotiate get what they ask for — employers budget for negotiation and the process is expected, not penalized
industry_realities.implication: Framing your counter professionally and with market data is sufficient to preserve the relationship while capturing significant value

industry_realities.common_belief: A manager's verbal promise of promotion is a commitment you can rely on
industry_realities.actual_reality: Verbal promotion promises are unenforceable — managers change, budgets shift, and criteria drift without written documentation; employees lose months or years waiting on promises that never materialize
industry_realities.implication: Always get promotion criteria, timeline, and comp expectations in writing before accepting any role change or continuing to wait for a promised promotion

industry_realities.common_belief: Generating urgency through a fake competing offer is a safe strategy
industry_realities.actual_reality: Recruiters verify competing offers, and fabricated offers are caught often enough that the risk is material; discovery leads to rescission and reputational damage
industry_realities.implication: Only use competing offer leverage when you have a real one; invest time in generating genuine competing offers rather than manufacturing fictitious ones

industry_realities.common_belief: Unspecified terms in an offer letter will be worked out after you join
industry_realities.actual_reality: Terms that are not in the offer letter are not commitments — verbal agreements made during recruitment have no enforceability after you sign
industry_realities.implication: Any agreed-upon term — signing bonus, remote work arrangement, in-office day count — must be in the written offer letter before you sign

industry_realities.common_belief: Relocation packages are straightforward dollar amounts you can spend on moving expenses
industry_realities.actual_reality: Post-2017 tax law makes relocation assistance taxable income, so a $10,000 relocation package may net only $6,000–$7,500 without a gross-up negotiation
industry_realities.implication: Always negotiate the gross amount of the relocation package and explicitly request a gross-up to cover the tax liability, not just the nominal dollar figure

industry_realities.common_belief: Under the H-1B lottery, salary negotiation and immigration strategy are separate concerns
industry_realities.actual_reality: Under the post-2025 wage-weighted lottery, negotiating for a higher wage level directly improves lottery odds — salary negotiation and immigration outcomes are structurally linked
industry_realities.implication: Frame salary negotiations in the context of wage level classification explicitly — a higher comp ask is simultaneously an immigration strategy, and both parties benefit from a Level III or IV classification.

industry_realities.common_belief: Exploding offer deadlines are genuine signals that the company needs a fast decision
industry_realities.actual_reality: Exploding offers are pressure tactics; virtually every one extends when the candidate explicitly calls it out and requests more time
industry_realities.implication: Never let an exploding offer deadline lapse silently; always request an extension explicitly and frame it around making an informed, committed decision

industry_realities.common_belief: The equity value the recruiter quotes is what the equity is worth
industry_realities.actual_reality: Recruiter-quoted equity valuations for pre-IPO companies are based on hoped-for future valuations, not current 409A values; early-stage equity should be valued at $0 for budgeting
industry_realities.implication: Apply stage-appropriate discount rates to all equity: public companies at 80-90% of market value, Series C-D at 60-90%, early-stage at $0 for planning purposes

industry_realities.common_belief: HR can always approve what a manager wants to pay
industry_realities.actual_reality: Salary bands structurally constrain what HR can approve regardless of manager intent — a manager who genuinely wants to pay you more may still be unable to do so within band limits
industry_realities.implication: Ask about salary band limits early in the negotiation to understand the structural ceiling, and factor this into whether the internal path can ever match external market

industry_realities.common_belief: Remote work is a lifestyle perk with no financial value
industry_realities.actual_reality: Remote work eliminates $2,000–$8,000/year in commuting costs and can provide a purchasing power equivalent of tens of thousands of dollars annually when working from a lower-cost city
industry_realities.implication: Remote work flexibility should be evaluated and negotiated as a financial benefit, not just a convenience preference

industry_realities.common_belief: You need a competing job offer to have real negotiating leverage
industry_realities.actual_reality: A BATNA can be any credible alternative you would genuinely pursue — another degree (resetting OPT clock), CPT positions, or another country's job market. It does not have to be a competing offer.
industry_realities.implication: International students who believe they have no leverage because they lack a competing offer may still have real alternatives they haven't articulated. Identify and document your actual BATNA before entering any negotiation.

industry_realities.common_belief: Salary is the main thing you can negotiate, and once it's fixed, negotiation is over
industry_realities.actual_reality: Companies often have far more flexibility on signing bonuses, equity, vacation days, professional development budgets, remote work, and project assignment than on base salary, which is constrained by pay bands and internal equity concerns
industry_realities.implication: When salary hits a ceiling, pivot immediately to other dimensions rather than accepting the ceiling as the end of the conversation

industry_realities.common_belief: Signing bonuses are part of your ongoing compensation
industry_realities.actual_reality: Signing bonuses are one-time payments; your year-2 and beyond compensation is materially lower unless the bonus is renewed, which is not standard
industry_realities.implication: Always model annual recurring compensation without the signing bonus to understand the true ongoing offer value; signing bonus is a bridge, not a salary component

industry_realities.common_belief: Having a competing offer is a form of bluffing or manipulation
industry_realities.actual_reality: Companies rationally respond to competing offers because a single interview is a weak signal of capability; multiple companies making offers is a much stronger combined signal — demand breeds demand
industry_realities.implication: Generating real competing offers through a serious parallel job search is both ethical and strategically essential; it is the most reliable lever available

industry_realities.common_belief: Providing your current salary when asked is a routine step that doesn't affect the outcome
industry_realities.actual_reality: Your current salary becomes the anchor for their offer; a company that knows you earn $70K will offer $75–80K even if they budgeted $95K, because your disclosure has justified underpaying you relative to market
industry_realities.implication: Deflect current salary questions using prepared scripts; the information asymmetry created by not disclosing is directly worth thousands of dollars

industry_realities.common_belief: A small salary increase is too trivial for a company to care about
industry_realities.actual_reality: Employers view employees at 150–200% loaded cost; they think about headcount budget in aggregate, not individual salaries; a $5K salary increase in their budget view is literally 'mouse droppings'
industry_realities.implication: Don't be embarrassed to make requests that seem large to you but are proportionally tiny in the company's budget context

industry_realities.common_belief: Large Canadian tech companies (Shopify, Amazon Canada, Google Canada) are the best first targets because of brand recognition and hiring volume
industry_realities.actual_reality: These companies receive flooded application pipelines and PGWP candidates without Canadian work experience or internal referrals are effectively invisible; mid-size companies (50–200 employees) in tech corridors have higher conversion rates for the same candidate profile
industry_realities.implication: PGWP job seekers should weight mid-size company applications more heavily and deprioritize large-brand cold applications, at least until a referral channel into those companies can be built

industry_realities.common_belief: International graduates in Canada face similar employer-side visa friction as international students in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: PGWP is an open work permit requiring zero employer action — it is functionally identical to domestic work authorization from the employer's perspective
industry_realities.implication: PGWP holders should present themselves as domestic candidates for work authorization purposes and not volunteer sponsorship language

industry_realities.common_belief: If a company says 'no sponsorship', international students cannot work there at all
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many companies that say 'no sponsorship' mean no H-1B petition specifically; F-1 OPT requires zero employer action, and STEM OPT extension requires only I-983 filing and E-Verify enrollment — which some of these companies will still do
industry_realities.implication: Candidates on OPT should not self-filter on 'no sponsorship' language without first clarifying what the company means; the phrase is ambiguous and recruiter knowledge is often incomplete

industry_realities.common_belief: HR is the right first contact when reaching out to a company about jobs
industry_realities.actual_reality: HR screens against quotas and sponsorship filters; hiring managers engage because they have a problem to solve and are motivated to find the right person regardless of friction
industry_realities.implication: Bypassing HR and emailing the hiring manager directly is more effective for cold outreach, especially for international candidates where HR will filter on sponsorship before evaluating skills

industry_realities.common_belief: Program prestige (ranking) is the primary signal for industry research job outcomes from a PhD
industry_realities.actual_reality: Industry research employers, especially FAANG and top AI labs, recruit from a wider range of programs than academic hiring does; advisor industry network and internship history are more predictive of placement than program rank alone
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should evaluate advisor-level industry connections as the primary filter, not just program rank — a rank-20 program with a well-connected advisor can outperform a rank-5 program with no industry ties

industry_realities.common_belief: If a company says they sponsor H-1B during the hiring process, you can rely on that commitment
industry_realities.actual_reality: Verbal promises of H-1B sponsorship are not legally binding; company immigration policies can change at any time due to budget cuts, legal risk reassessment, or leadership changes, with no obligation to employees who were verbally promised sponsorship
industry_realities.implication: Every new offer negotiation should include a demand for explicit written sponsorship language in the offer letter as a non-negotiable condition — relying on verbal assurances or company reputation is a structural risk

industry_realities.common_belief: Equity compensation from tech companies is essentially free money on top of your salary
industry_realities.actual_reality: RSU vesting is a taxable event at ordinary income rates; in California, combined federal + state tax can consume ~40-50% of the vested value immediately, and ISO options carry potential AMT liability that can exceed the actual cash value of the shares
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should model after-tax equity value — not gross grant value — when comparing offers; the stated RSU value in an offer letter is not what you will actually receive

industry_realities.common_belief: Keeping your current salary secret gives you more negotiating power
industry_realities.actual_reality: Multiple HR commenters stated that current salary disclosure is standard practice, verified through background checks and payslip requests at offer stage — fabricating or withholding it only damages trust and can cause offer rescission
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should disclose current salary accurately, but shift the conversation toward future value and market benchmarks rather than anchoring solely on the current number

industry_realities.common_belief: Pick the offer with the highest total compensation number
industry_realities.actual_reality: Total comp numbers are misleading without applying personal importance weights; and a higher-paying offer in a lower-value role can produce lower lifetime earnings than a lower-paying offer in a high-value role
industry_realities.implication: You need a weighted scoring model calibrated to your own priorities, not just a raw comp comparison

industry_realities.common_belief: If you perform well after joining, the company will raise your salary to match peers who started at a higher base
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most companies — especially large or publicly listed ones — apply raises as a fixed percentage tied to a performance band. A lower base means even an identical performance rating yields a lower absolute raise. The starting gap widens over time, not narrows.
industry_realities.implication: The only reliable moment to close a compensation gap is at the offer stage. Candidates should treat the offer negotiation as their primary leverage window, not a preliminary round before the 'real' negotiation inside the job.

industry_realities.common_belief: You should not negotiate after receiving an offer because it will make you look difficult and the company will rescind the offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: HR's KPI is to hire the right person within budget — losing a good candidate over a small salary gap is worse for them than adjusting the number. Informed commenters from both China and US contexts agree: negotiating at the offer stage is expected, especially for experienced hires
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should negotiate without guilt; the fear of rescission is almost always unfounded for reasonable asks backed by market data

industry_realities.common_belief: The RSU grant amount in your offer letter is the number of shares you'll receive
industry_realities.actual_reality: The offer letter states a dollar value; the actual share count is calculated on your first day of employment based on the stock's closing price that day (or a recent average, per company policy). The share count is not known at offer acceptance
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should model scenarios where the stock price moves between signing and start date, and should not fixate on a specific share count until Day 1

industry_realities.common_belief: HR's stated maximum salary or raise cap is a fixed company policy that cannot be exceeded
industry_realities.actual_reality: HR often has a personal approval limit below the true ceiling; exceeding it requires going to a higher manager for special approval, which HR will do if the candidate is strong enough and they are motivated to close
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should not accept HR's first ceiling as final — they should give HR the motivation and supporting evidence to escalate by making the case for their own value clearly
industry_realities._source: zhihu_面试时谈薪的技巧有些什么啊.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian employers understand what a PGWP is and know it doesn't require sponsorship
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many Canadian employers — including hiring managers and recruiters at otherwise sophisticated companies — conflate 'work permit' with 'requires sponsorship' and filter out candidates preemptively; this was confirmed across multiple high-upvote comments
industry_realities.implication: PGWP holders must treat work authorization education as their own responsibility and proactively use specific, unambiguous language in every application touchpoint

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting a tech job in Canada is equally accessible from any Canadian city
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canada's tech market is smaller and heavily concentrated in Toronto and Vancouver; candidates in other cities face significantly thinner opportunity sets
industry_realities.implication: Geographic flexibility or deliberate relocation to major hubs is a meaningful lever for job search outcomes, especially in a smaller national market

industry_realities.common_belief: Asking about sponsorship is inherently risky and should be avoided as long as possible
industry_realities.actual_reality: Avoiding the conversation entirely creates larger risks — wasted interview cycles and late-stage rejections after significant investment by both parties; informed commenters agree disclosure before offer acceptance is the correct timing
industry_realities.implication: The risk is not in asking — it's in asking too early. Frame the conversation factually and without apology in final rounds

industry_realities.common_belief: More information in a cold email signals stronger candidacy
industry_realities.actual_reality: Cold emails over 150 words are routinely skimmed or deleted; brevity is a signal of communication skill and respect for the recipient's time, not a sign of weak candidacy
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should cut cold emails to under 100 words and trust the call to carry the detail

industry_realities.common_belief: A PhD will improve your compensation and career trajectory regardless of the role you end up in
industry_realities.actual_reality: The PhD compensation premium is concentrated in research scientist roles; for standard software engineering positions, the premium is minimal to nonexistent, and the opportunity cost of 4-5 years of foregone industry salary and equity typically outweighs any benefit
industry_realities.implication: The decision to pursue a PhD should be gated on whether the target role actually requires or substantially rewards the credential — not assumed to be universally beneficial

industry_realities.common_belief: L-1 and O-1 visas are realistic fallback options for most tech workers who lose H-1B sponsorship
industry_realities.actual_reality: L-1 requires 1+ year of employment abroad with the same multinational employer; O-1 requires genuinely extraordinary ability with documented evidence — the vast majority of tech workers do not qualify for either
industry_realities.implication: Workers on OPT should not build contingency plans around L-1 or O-1 unless they have already verified eligibility with an immigration attorney; the realistic fallbacks are new H-1B sponsors, cap-exempt employers, or returning to school

industry_realities.common_belief: Stock options are always better than RSU because they have more upside
industry_realities.actual_reality: Options require capital outlay to exercise, carry more complex tax exposure (especially ISO/AMT), expire after departure (often 90 days), and are worth zero if the stock doesn't rise above the strike price; RSU have lower ceiling but guaranteed value as long as the stock has any value
industry_realities.implication: For employees who are not early-stage founders or very early employees, RSU is often the lower-risk, more predictable form of equity compensation; options are higher variance in both directions

industry_realities.common_belief: HR is the adversary in salary negotiation — their job is to pay you as little as possible
industry_realities.actual_reality: HR commenters across the thread explained that HR's actual goal is to find a match point between candidate expectations and hiring team budget — they are intermediaries, not opponents, and a candidate who makes their job easy (clear expectations, honest data) gets better advocacy
industry_realities.implication: Treating HR as a collaborator and communicating clearly about your expectations improves your outcome more than treating them adversarially

industry_realities.common_belief: Big company always beats small company because of brand and stability
industry_realities.actual_reality: Large companies can have very low internal mobility — employees stagnating at the same level for 3-4 years with low salary growth; a smaller company with fast promotion cycles may produce better career and financial outcomes
industry_realities.implication: You must research actual promotion velocity at the specific large company, not just assume prestige = growth

industry_realities.common_belief: Re-negotiating after receiving a formal offer is risky because the company will see it as bad faith or opportunistic
industry_realities.actual_reality: This belief is stated in the top answer but presented as a personal opinion with zero upvotes and no corroboration. It may reflect a specific cultural or market context (likely China domestic) rather than a universal rule. In many professional markets, post-offer negotiation is standard and expected.
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should not treat this framing as a universal rule. Context — country, industry, seniority level, and whether a competing offer exists — heavily determines how post-offer negotiation is received.

industry_realities.common_belief: You can negotiate a salary adjustment after probation by making an informal agreement with the recruiter or manager
industry_realities.actual_reality: Large companies have rigid salary adjustment windows (typically annual or semi-annual reviews) and the labor contract already specifies the salary; informal pre-hire verbal promises are legally unenforceable and HR departments cannot act on them outside the formal cycle
industry_realities.implication: Never trade away the offer-stage negotiation for a vague post-probation promise; get any adjustment commitment in writing in the offer letter or do not accept it as a real commitment
